e865223d2891cc3d: MADRID: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono said Wednesday he is enduring the "hardest days of my life" after the death of Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, whom he collided with during a Spanish second division match on Monday.

The 30-year-old Spanish footballer died Tuesday as a result of injuries he suffered in the sickening collision with Equatorial Guinea international Owono, who had raced into midfield to clear an aerial ball.
"These are the hardest days of my life. I struggle to find the words and it is very difficult for me to process anything that has happened," said Owono in a statement published by his club Andorra.
"I feel immense pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, of his family, and of all the people who loved him.

"I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are going through. Rest in peace, Jesus."
Spanish police sources told AFP an investigation into what happened has been opened, under judicial supervision.
Andorra players observed a minute's silence on Wednesday before a voluntary training session, which Owono, 25, did not attend.
Owono received support from the president of the African country's federation, Venancio Tomas Micha, in a letter of condolence following De Miguel's death.
"I feel compelled to convey all our solidarity and support at this time to our player Jesus Lazaro Owono," Tomas Micha wrote.
"We know that, as the involuntary protagonist of this tragic incident in the game, he is living through this situation with deep sorrow and distress.
"From the Equatorial Guinea Football Federation, we offer him all our human and professional backing, fully aware of the harshness of this event, which no one in our sport ever wishes to witness."
Andorra defender Lautaro Spatz posted on Instagram in support of Owono, whom he said was "deeply affected" by what had happened.
"Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone," wrote Spatz.
"In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."
Postponements
Earlier it was confirmed Tenerife and Andorra's Spanish second division matches scheduled for the weekend would be postponed.
Tenerife were due to face Granada away from home, while Andorra were set to welcome Mallorca.
"After the tragic news of the death of Tenerife player Jesus de Miguel, the game... this Saturday Nov 7, at Nuevo Los Carmenes (stadium), has been postponed," said Granada in a statement.
Mallorca said "at times like this, respect and sensitivity in the face of a situation of profound grief must come first".
The Spanish football federation postponed all Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina matches this week as a mark of respect following De Miguel's death.
Tenerife plan to hold a tribute to De Miguel at the club's stadium on Saturday which supporters can attend, and are holding a six-day mourning period.
The club said the first team, board and staff will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, in the province of Toledo on the Spanish mainland, where he has family roots.

A minute of silence was held before Champions League matches on Tuesday in honour of the striker, with the same planned for the rest of the week's fixtures organised by European football governing body Uefa.
bbcef06b4e6a0b68: WASHINGTON: The US on Wednesday issued sanctions targeting what it described as a "vast criminal network" run by two Indian nationals that was aiding Iran's shadow fleet of oil tankers in committing maritime fraud.
In a statement, the US Treasury said the network aided Iranian vessels in sailing under false flags and in gaining fake maritime certifications.

The move was the latest in a tightening web of US sanctions targeting Iran since August, when Washington announced that it would be seeking the "economic asphyxiation" of the country in conjunction with its military campaign.

The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran in late February, plunging the Middle East into violence as Tehran's retaliatory action struck US allies and closed a vital energy trade waterway.

"As we have said many times, under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us," said Treasury secretary Scott Bessent, who has in the past threatened sanctions against any country or company that aids Iran, regardless of its relationship with Washington.
"We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air."
Wednesday's sanctions named Indian nationals Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife Jaspreet Preeti Shahid as operating a large-scale maritime fraud network from their base in Chandigarh.

"Purporting to represent nations from nearly every continent, from Guyana to Eswatini and Laos, Sharma and Shahid have allowed the Iranian shadow fleet... to evade international restrictions on their operation," the Treasury said in a statement.
The sanctions also targeted two other Indian nationals and a number of companies Treasury said were part of the criminal network.

Wednesday's action also saw Washington sanction Turkey-based Fugo Ground Services Inc for allegedly continuing to provide services to Iran's aviation sector, which the United States has sought to shut down.
Earlier this month, the United States imposed sanctions targeting "the remnants of Iran's shadow fleet" of tankers used to transport oil products to foreign markets, affecting 17 vessels.

e73411ab81c4d157: WASHINGTON: US president Donald Trump concedes that the war he ordered on Iran was partly to blame for his Republican Party's sweeping midterms losses -- but even as he comes under pressure, analysts said Wednesday that he has few good options ahead.
It remains to be seen what path Trump will take after emerging politically weakened as Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's vote.

The US leader also remains caught between a desire to diplomatically end the war with Iran -- which has sharply driven up gasoline costs for American voters -- and his threats to "finish it off" with Tehran.

"Trump is now in a bind: Escalation offers no clear path to victory and risks further wrecking his presidency, while diplomacy offers a potential way out," said Sina Toossi, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy.
"The new Democratic Congress will also have significant oversight and funding powers come January, further constraining his options," Toossi told AFP.
Trump acknowledged Wednesday that "it's largely true" that Iran and the high fuel prices provoked by the conflict had led to the massive defeat for Republicans.
Still, he maintained, echoing a similar statement after polls closed Tuesday, that he'd "do it again" despite the election hammering.
Vice-president JD Vance, a potential contender to succeed Trump in the 2028 presidential election, was more definitive.
"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote in a post on X.
A 'clear' message
Many American voters cited high costs of living and the Iran war as reasons behind their vote.

For usually reliable Republican voters, like farmers, steep energy costs are "really just leading to despair," Charles Hall, executive director of the North Carolina Soybean Producers Association, told AFP.
Hall, a North Carolina voter himself, noted huge shifts towards Democrats in his state: "That tells me that they're voting against something."
"If they're farmers, they're probably voting against high diesel prices," Hall said.
Tehran retaliated against US-Israel strikes on Iran since late February by blocking off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global energy transit. This sent oil prices soaring.
But Council on Foreign Relations senior fellow James Lindsay told AFP that "the historic drubbing that Republicans took on election day happened for reasons that go well beyond Iran."
He called the "blue tsunami" a repudiation of much of Trump's agenda, with the president being elected in 2024 on a pledge to make life more affordable.

"What we've seen over the past two years is that Americans believe that life has become even more unaffordable," Lindsay told AFP. "The Iran war clearly played into that by driving up the price of gas and diesel."
Adding fuel to fire, Trump has "often behaved in ways that suggested he was indifferent to the pain and suffering of Americans," he said.
Toossi added: "The message from voters is clear: They want relief from the war's economic costs, not more war."
'Difficult position'
Already, top Senate Democrat Chuck Schumer said Wednesday that the Iran war "must end," with prospective Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries echoing a similar message.
But it remains unclear if Trump will listen to voters and try to end the conflict quickly, or push on with it.
"Putting aside the election, doubling down on Iran was always a dangerous strategy," Lindsay of CFR said.
A new round of intense attacks -- even if designed to be short-term -- could backfire with Iranians responded by targeting installations across the Gulf.
"This could spiral out of control," he added, although acknowledging that Trump's other options "aren't terribly good either."
Meanwhile, maintaining the US naval blockade in the Middle East is a strain on the country's military, while negotiations have so far failed to yield clear progress.
"The president's in a difficult position regardless," Lindsay said.
And if Vance's comments on the war are widely held by other Republican lawmakers, he added, Trump faces new political risks if he were to double down on Iran.
1c4e923017412ae9: WASHINGTON: US vice-president JD Vance said Wednesday that the Iran war had doomed Republicans in the midterm elections, moving to distance himself from the unpopular conflict ahead of a possible 2028 White House run.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance said in a lengthy post on X -- apparently referring to President Donald Trump's remarks that the Iran war was "part of it" but that it was still justified.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," added Vance.
"But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
The Democratic wave in Tuesday's midterms has raised major questions over Vance's previous status as the frontrunner for the Republican nomination in the 2028 presidential election.
He has not yet formally declared that he will run.
Vance, a longtime vocal critic of US foreign interventionism, had reportedly been skeptical behind the scenes about the war on Iran that Trump and Israel launched in late February.
Vance also acknowledged that Republican voters who backed Trump and himself two years ago had switched sides due to the war and its effects on the US economy.
"The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026," Vance said.
He said a pollster that he respected showed the Iran war and the economy were key factors in voters abandoning Republicans, along with a desire to "change our relationship to Israel".
9a48a448a5c35f9c: ISTANBUL: Dirk Kuyt got the better of his former club Liverpool as Fenerbahce twice came from behind for a famous 3-2 win in Istanbul on Wednesday that breathed new life into their Champions League campaign.
Liverpool had won their opening three European games under Andoni Iraola, but were punished for sloppy defending in a surprise defeat.
Trey Nyoni and substitute Alexander Isak twice put the visitors in front.
But Liverpool, who lost twice away to Galatasaray last season, were beaten again in Istanbul as Englishmen Mason Greenwood and Archie Brown levelled before Vedat Muriqi's winner.
"We've gone twice in front after having good moments, controlling the game, we've found the goals but after we've conceded in situations we should definitely defend better," said Iraola.
Fenerbahce's interim boss Kuyt, who spent six years at Anfield as a player, was taking charge for just the second time after Ismail Kartal quit last week.
The Turkish giants had taken just two points from their opening three Champions League games but made the most of Liverpool's generosity at the back.
Liverpool's perfect Champions League start allowed Iraola the luxury of leaving out Isak and Florian Wirtz among five changes from Sunday's 1-0 defeat by Arsenal.
Nyoni retained his place and capped another fine performance with his first Liverpool goal from the edge of the box after Fenerbahce failed to clear Dominik Szoboszlai's cross.
The home side bounced back just four minutes later when Alisson Becker was deceived by Greenwood's deflected free-kick to equalise.
Iraola unleashed Isak, Wirtz and Cody Gakpo from the bench just after the hour mark in search of a winner and got an almost immediate reward.
Isak was afforded far too much space to head in Gakpo's cross.
But again Liverpool quickly handed back their advantage.
Gakpo's touch inadvertently deflected a cross beyond Alisson to give Brown an easy tap-in at the back post.
Liverpool then conceded for the 10th time in four Champions League games when Muriqi outmuscled Jeremy Jacquet to a looping cross and steered a header into the bottom corner.
Defeat cost Liverpool the chance to move level with Paris Saint-Germain at the top of the Champions League table.

"I think we've put ourselves in good positions, so that today if we lose this game it's not a chaos situation," said Isak. "We just need to get back to winning ways and if we win the next game, we are back to a really good position."
Victory moves Fenerbahce move up to 19th in the 36-team table.
Only the top eight qualify directly for the last 16 with ninth to 24th facing off in a two-legged play-off.

1eebb3be60c9a4b7: WASHINGTON: US House speaker Mike Johnson will step down as Republican leader following his party's crushing midterm election defeat, his spokesman confirmed to AFP Wednesday.
Johnson, the highest-ranking Republican in the US after President Donald Trump and vice-president JD Vance, is second in the line of presidential succession.
Asked whether reports that Johnson would step aside were correct, his spokesman responded in a one-word email: "Accurate".
The Louisiana Republican told staff of his decision Wednesday morning, a day after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress in a sweeping rejection of Trump's party.
Johnson, 54, had led the House since October 2023, when he emerged as a compromise candidate after weeks of Republican infighting following the ouster of his predecessor, Kevin McCarthy.
He had campaigned extensively to preserve the Republicans' narrow House majority and previously suggested he might remain party leader even if Democrats won control.
His decision not to seek the minority leadership clears the way for a contest between current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee chairman Jim Jordan.
Johnson won reelection to his Louisiana seat, and his decision does not mean he is immediately resigning as speaker or leaving Congress.
1a40bd67518646ec: ATHENS: Federico Valverde lashed home a stunning effort from distance to snatch Real Madrid a late 3-2 victory at AEK Athens on Wednesday in the Champions League and preserve their 100% start.

Jose Mourinho's side twice came from behind against the Greek champions before Valverde claimed all three points for his side, level with holders Paris Saint-Germain on four wins from four league phase games.
Aboubakary Koita sent AEK ahead after 12 minutes and Jude Bellingham equalised with a sublime flick for the record 15-time winners.
Stavros Pilios sent the Greek champions ahead with 15 minutes to go but Kylian Mbappe swiftly pulled Madrid level once again, setting the stage for Valverde's late winner.
"Fede has that capability... (but) I didn't ask him to shoot," Mourinho told Movistar about his match-winner, who came on in the second half.

"I told him was that the game was wide open, it was being played at great speed... a fresh player like Fede, with his ability to cover a lot of ground, I told him to attack the space and arrive in the dangerous areas."
Madrid have now won seven straight games across all competitions.
"We fought for (the victory), and with the score at 2–2 we didn't settle," added Mourinho.
"It would always be an acceptable result, we'd be on 10 points, but we wanted more."
Mourinho started with Vinicius Junior on the left flank, after he missed the team's previous two matches through suspension, in LaLiga.
The hosts started with huge energy at the Agia Sophia stadium and it was not overly surprising when they took an early lead.
Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois saved well from former Los Blancos striker Luka Jovic before Koita sent AEK ahead.
The Mauritanian winger shifted cleverly inside Marc Cucurella and thumped home at the near post, catching out Courtois.
The Belgian goalkeeper saved again from Jovic as AEK tried to make their strong start count.
However they inevitably began to tire and Madrid began to take the reins in the Greek capital.
Kylian Mbappe fired over and Bellingham netted from close range but was shown to be offside. Moments later the England international scored again and nobody could deny him this one.
Cucurella fired in a low cross and Bellingham produced a brilliant flicked finish to beat goalkeeper Alberto Brignoli.
Former Chelsea defender Cucurella tested Brignoli and Bernardo Silva nodded off-target before the interval as Mourinho's team controlled the game.
Brignoli pushed away Eder Militao's long-range effort early in the second half and Lazaros Rota blocked superbly to deny the heavily-involved Cucurella.
Another fightback
Mbappe bent a shot narrowly wide of the top corner with Italian stopper Brignoli at full stretch.
The France forward was frustrated by the AEK defence when Vinicius turned sharply and found him with a high pass, but the striker's shot was blocked.
AEK reclaimed the lead in the 75th minute when the impressive Koita gently nudged the ball into Pilios's path and the Albania international finished through Courtois's legs from close range.
Madrid immediately responded with Bellingham playing Denzel Dumfries in down the right. The Netherlands defender rolled a low ball across the six-yard box and this time Mbappe was able to finish.
It was Mbappe's fourth goal in four Champions League games this season, netting once in each, and his 16th across all competitions.
Madrid substitute Endrick sent Mbappe through on goal with five minutes remaining but Brignoli produced a sensational save to tip his strike against the crossbar.
Valverde refused to give up on the three points and in the 92nd minute he lashed home across Brignoli to keep Madrid perfect.
Koita, who had been substituted, was sent off after the game for apparent dissent.
Valverde thanked his team-mates for backing him when he gets the chance to shoot.

"Sometimes I overthink it, and well, as I always say, I'm grateful to the players, to my teammates, because they're the ones who give me the confidence so that, in those moments, I can make that decision and have the courage to hit it," he said.

da017af7ff0478cd: Alex Karp, CEO of US spy-tech company Palantir, used this week's historic US midterm election results to claim an unlikely mantle for a military software supplier: pioneer of an antiwar movement.

Palantir's Q3 revenue rose 96 percent year-on-year to $2.31 billion, although its shares fell 8 percent following the results, which it reported on Tuesday as US voters were delivering a resounding defeat for Republicans in the voting booth. For Karp, the figures represented "the reality that this moment has become a real focal point of understanding" and might help explain "what is happening in our society."
From the CEO's perspective, they not only reflected the company's financial performance, but also its overall "mission."

"That mission reason is we support your alpha [above average performance], we support your sovereignty. We support the war fighter. We are delighted that we can support the war fighter even more because we're making so much money. But we believe we have a moral imperative to be the dominant player in our industry," he told investors.
For Karp-watchers, this is familiar self-serving shtick: turn Palantir's work for military and intelligence customers into a moral crusade, and goad its critics along the way.

"There's this larger question of what does it mean to have a business that was built around what we believed and believe now is the most important mission in the world, supporting our war fighters, [and] bringing them home," he said.
None of this stops him presenting Palantir as a force for peace. "We see ourselves as the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement," he wrote in his shareholder letter.

He expanded on the point during the Q3 earnings call. "Our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that, in fact, it's not worth going to war and also to create social cohesion because we're going to bring back our troops healthier, safer, undamaged and that makes our society much more effective," he said.

That antiwar pitch sits awkwardly alongside Karp's $1 million donation in December 2024 to MAGA Inc., the super PAC supporting Donald Trump. Trump subsequently launched a US military operation in Venezuela and went to war with Iran, repeatedly promising the latter conflict would be short-lived as it dragged on. Karp did not address either topic on the call.

Elsewhere, Karp claimed that Palantir "built products that would protect civil liberties and stop terrorism. If you don't stop terrorism, you're going to get a radical fringe on the right. If you stop terrorism without rights, none of us wants that."

That civil liberties pitch also invites scrutiny of Palantir's longstanding relationship with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), whose treatment of people it targets and detains has drawn criticism from US judges.

Karp seems to enjoy the circus of controversy he and his colleagues have created. He also offered investors this insight: "The future is becoming the present and the present is now." Whatever that future holds, he seems confident Palantir has a moral imperative to invoice it. ®

eeff4737bf340d02: Voters respond to economic and political messages and experiences. AP Photo/Lindsey WassonAs Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise. Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C. Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers, with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on. When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally. Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection. For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record. Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections. Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%. When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3%, and gas prices were still high. Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “Whip Inflation Now,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats. “WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter. Carter’s struggles In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly. Inflation hit 9% in 1978. In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats. Inflation continued to climb, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan. Reagan enters the picture Reagan implemented “Reaganomics” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum. By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut, lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs. In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate. Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate. Trump’s first round In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22%. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate. Democratic Party supporters react to the results of the 2018 midterm elections, when their party won control of the U.S. House of Representatives. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images Biden years Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups. And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon. Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies. Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon. But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source. In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today. The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots. Trump’s second term During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5%, U.S. oil production rose 3.3%, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon. On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted, though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels. Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026. Implications As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices, as well as an unpopular war. It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future, they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties. Michael A. 938f3cec510e6579: Fedora 45 is here, after not one but two week-long delays as the team found last-minute issues. Although both the original and second announcements were irksomely non-specific, in general we prefer this "when it's ready" approach to the rigid calendar-based schedule that Canonical favors for Ubuntu. It includes six main editions, five immutable desktop variants, and 12 "spins" with different GUIs.

The combined version 45 release notes detail some of the bigger individual component changes and note the hardware requirements. The recommended spec is now a 2 GHz quad-core CPU with 8 GB of RAM and 20 GB of disk space, and at least 1024×768 graphics. Fedora 45 supports most display adapters, but 3D acceleration may not work on older GPUs, including Intel models prior to GMA9xx, Nvidia models prior to NV30 (GeForce FX5xxx series), and AMD Radeon models prior to R300 (Radeon 9500).

We took a quick look at the beta back in September, focusing on its new next-generation text console, which is a welcome change. We especially liked the ability to zoom in and out on the text console on the fly, which is something we've missed since the superb "Laptop Ultravision" for DOS, about a third of a century ago. (The company is long gone, but we found a downloadable version for all you DOS users.)

The desktop flagship editions are Workstation 45, which comes with GNOME 51 "A Coruña", and Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop, with KDE Plasma 6.8. We covered some of the new features in GNOME 51 when we looked at the Ubuntu 26.10 beta, and those changes apply here too – notably, improvements in the Settings app, but removal of some older Nvidia GPU support.

Both the big names are Wayland-only environments now, but by our reckoning, X11 fans have seven of the 12 official spins to choose from: Xfce, Cinnamon, MATE, i3, LXQt, LXDE, and Sugar (SOAS) all still use X.org if you prefer. There is also a combined What's New page for all the Atomic Desktops, Fedora’s immutable variants – the main shared feature here being the new web-based installer.

The new version of main Fedora is accompanied by Fedora Asahi Remix 45 for Apple Silicon Macs. This is a more notable release than the cross-platform editions, as Asahi 45 brings initial support for M3-based Macs as well as M1 and M2 kit. As The Reg described in September, though, the M3 support is preliminary and limited – for instance, it excludes the M3 Ultra. If you have an M3 Mac, for now, you're better off sticking to macOS.

The most important changes in Fedora 45 are under the hood, which is what the Red Hat release announcement focuses on. It now uses RPM version 6.1, with enhanced package signature checking, and blocks the vendor of packages silently changing. The GNOME keyring now uses the oo7 secrets manager. Support for two old VPN plugins has been removed, because the packages were unmaintained.

A feature that we are happy to see land at last is better support for Red Hat’s Stratis next-generation storage subsystem. We gave a potted overview of Stratis 3.3 back in 2022: it was on version 3.3 back then. It’s the same main Stratis version 3.9 we saw in Fedora 44, but the installation program now has support for installing Fedora 45 on Stratis storage.

Stratis is Red Hat’s rival to OpenZFS. The plan is that Stratis offers similar features and resilience to ZFS, especially in the field of copy-on-write snapshots and simple multi-device logical volume management, but built from all-GPL code. Rather than a whole new filesystem, Stratis integrates XFS, LVM, and the kernel device-mapper functionality. Stratis 1.0 appeared in Fedora 29 eight years ago, and Fedora 45 has version 3.9.3. It's good to see it finally making real progress: if nothing else, we've seen Btrfs irretrievably corrupt a full volume far too many times to ever trust it again, so an alternative is very welcome.

When we looked at Fedora 44, we noted the difficulty of doing custom disk partitioning. It was there, but very well-hidden. Now, the installer can launch the Cockpit web-management tool to make it easier to set up your drives however you want.

An interesting side-effect of the delayed release is that Fedora 45 ships with kernel 7.2 – specifically, version 7.2.15, which is the last release of this short-term series. In other words, it’s an end-of-life kernel version. It’s an amusing contrast to its near-contemporary Ubuntu 26.10, which shipped with a pre-release kernel. Our test Ubuntu box was automatically upgraded to the release version by the background automatic updates process, but to our surprise, it didn't receive the kernel update for over a week. This shouldn't be a problem: unlike Ubuntu, Fedora releases routinely receive updates to whole new kernel versions, so we’re sure Fedora 45 users will get kernel 7.3 very soon.

We upgraded the same test machine on which we tried GNOME 48 in Fedora 42 early last year. You can skip one Fedora release on upgrade, but not two, so we had to go via Fedora 44 — which took some time, and threw up a minor packaging glitch, but it got there. The result runs surprisingly well, although this 2008 machine is well below the recommended spec. ®

31bba1eca5b3b896: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail.

Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities, began changing course himself.

Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.

The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium.

That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.

The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects.

Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it.
A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.

It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.

This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.

Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

2c5a7beab5e34e66: Your new robot servant doesn't have to look anything like a person or walk on two legs. In fact, it might just be a claw that hangs from the ceiling instead.

That’s the future envisioned by Nathaniel Nifong, founder of Neufangled Robotics, and its Stringman robot. Put simply, Stringman is an AI-equipped claw suspended from four strings running through the corners of a room (up to 10 meters diagonally). Two motorized anchors adjust the lengths of the strings to move the claw around the room, from ceilings up to 4 meters high down to the floor to pick stuff up. With a payload capacity of around 2 kg, depending on its position, Stringman can move items to designated locations – like a toy box – and perform tidying tasks.
Stringman can also be manually controlled if you’d prefer to play a room-sized crane game by yourself.

According to Stringman’s documentation site, the device is currently a public prototype that “can self-calibrate in a new room and run policies, but is not yet reliable enough to be called a home appliance.”
That said, demonstration videos on the website show it in action, and it’s neat to watch.

Stringman is shown picking up laundry and dropping it in a basket, putting Lego bricks and other kids' toys back where they belong, and generally zooming around rooms and demonstrating its agility. One could imagine a properly trained Stringman could even grab the remote you left on the other side of the living room and drop it in your waiting hand if you’re that incredibly lazy.

“Our mission is to give people an organized home,” Neufangled says on its future roadmap page. “We prioritize robots that are narrowly effective at something that helps today rather than a general purpose robot that may be in development for years.”

The company further describes its goal as designing robots that are low cost and capable of doing things that people hate to do - e.g., pick up after a messy toddler - and making a robot that can do that while camouflaging itself into the home “as well as possible.”
As long as you think a foot-long claw robot hanging from the corner of the ceiling is camouflaged, this is the robot for you.

Neufangled lists Stringman for $795, which is a lot to ask for a public prototype that isn’t reliable enough to be called a home appliance yet. Luckily for those who’re interested in this sort of niche home automation, it’s fully open source, too.

“A complete Stringman is three Raspberry Pis on your Wi-Fi network,” the documentation site reads: One in the gripper, and two in the corner anchor mounts that store line reels and have cameras to track the claw’s location as it moves around the room. A third camera mounted on the claw provides visual feedback. Oh, you'll also need a dedicated PC or Mac to run the robot's motion-control software.

As for Stringman itself, to build your own, you'll need a 3D printer, a supplier to manufacture the PCBs, motors, Raspberry Pis, and other components listed in the bill of materials. You'll also need to follow the guides on the documentation site to get it up and running, calibrate it for your space using printed markers, set up drop-off points using visual tags, and program it to perform tasks.

But is it safe? One could imagine getting tangled in the lines if you get in Stringman’s way. Nifong admits that can happen, writing in the documentation that he has walked into the lines himself without injury.

“I live with two of these, and I've walked into the lines before. It's startling, but harmless — they're light and they give,” he writes. According to the robot’s website, it has a tension limit of 28 newtons, or around six and a quarter pounds of force. If that limit is reached, all of the lines relax and can be pulled loose.

e5014ca6bf0248e9: Scientists have developed a way to remove starlight from telescope images that improved sensitivity to faint exoplanets by up to 15 times in tests on James Webb Space Telescope data.
A team led by Northwestern University's Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez combined a physics-based telescope model with optimization techniques used in machine learning to subtract unwanted starlight.

Directly imaging exoplanets remains difficult because their host stars' glare can overwhelm their faint light. Existing techniques subtract modeled or reference starlight, but tiny changes in telescope optics can leave residual glare that hides planets.
The team's Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP) framework models how light passes through the telescope, adjusts for optical imperfections, and simulates the glare to be subtracted.

Applied to observations from Webb's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam), FLIP produced the first image of the known giant planet 51 Eridani b at an infrared wavelength of 4.3 micrometers, where conventional processing had failed. Tests showed sensitivity improvements of two to 15 times over conventional techniques, according to the Nature paper.

"This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories… potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success," the paper says.
Further work includes reducing computational demands and developing ways to handle the much larger data volumes produced by ground-based observations.
The researchers hope further development and testing will bring direct images of Earth-like planets closer, while reducing the extent to which tiny telescope instabilities obscure them. ®

96824d6c1d2d1d4e: <!--kg-card-end: html--> People across America rejected data centers during last night’s midterm election. Proposals related to data centers were explicitly on the ballot in more than 40 races across 13 states. People voted against data centers in 38 of them and counting. Six cities voted to ban data centers outright and 12 put limits on the amount of megawatts such buildings could draw. In addition to specific ballot measures, candidates who supported data centers lost across the country.

One of the most striking repudiations of pro data center politicians was in Texas, where Gregg Abbott lost a bid for a fourth term as governor. Abbott had made Texas a data center friendly place. The state has more than 300 working data centers and there are plans to double that number. “Texas is the epicenter of AI development,” Abbott said in 2025 at a press conference with Google CEO Sundar Pichai. “We must ensure that America remains at the forefront of the AI revolution, and Texas is the place where that can happen.” He went on to accept more than $9 million from data center-related donors.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> When public sentiment turned against data centers, Abbott attempted to ride shifting political winds by issuing a “pause” on new projects. The pause wasn’t real. Texas regulators continued to approve data center projects after Abbott’s announcement and only shut down the state’s permitting web portal when 404 Media reported it.

Gina Hinojosa, Texas’s Democratic governor-elect, made Abbott’s stance on data centers a central part of her campaign. Abbott’s words about making Texas a data center-friendly AI state played on TVs and the internet over and over again. He lost by more than 700,000 votes.

Anti-data center candidates overwhelmingly won statewide races across the country. In Burgin, Kentucky, mayoral candidate George Hensley lost his bid after voting to approve a hyperscale project—to a write-in candidate. Hensley was the only name on the ballot, and he lost to Joe MonroeTK, who ran an anti-data center write-in campaign. Emporia, Kansas — where police arrested a school teacher for clapping during a data center related city meeting — passed a ban on high impact data centers. In Yukon, Oklahoma the mayor lost a recall election after he supported a hyperscale data center project.

"These midterms sent a clear message — people don't want to see data centers in their backyards,” Michael Whitesides, the deputy communications director for Local Progress, told 404 Media. “Across the country, people do not see the promised benefit of these data centers, and the AI they power, playing out in their daily lives. They're seeing basic goods and services get more expensive while these billionaire backed monstrosities take up space in their community, poison their air, and drive up their utility bills.”

Local Progress is a network of local elected officials. Over the past year, its members have become increasingly focused on data centers as a top political issue. “Last night, we saw local, state, and federal officials who backed data center deals lose their seats,” Whitesides said. He noted that Kim Rooney in Asheville, North Carolina and Amanda Rodrigues in San Marcos, Texas (both members of Local Progress) were elected mayors in their cities after running anti-data center campaigns.

“Big Tech will continue its typical playbook of trying to buy and bully local officials into complying with their demands for more data center development, but our hope is that last night's results are a clear signal to local leaders that they can resist and their community will back them up,” Whitesides said.

American voters in the communities where they’re being built hate data centers. They run up power bills, burn through water, and power Silicon Valley’s AI apparatus. America rejected data centers last night as both symbols of the big tech oligarchy and a physical manifestation of the future it wants to build. It’s a future Americans seem willing to fight.

Elon Musk, one of the night’s big losers, took a break from a weeks-long posting spree on X as the election results rolled in. Musk spent half a billion dollars on the midterms, $224 of it in Texas, the state where he lives and does a lot of business. The world’s richest man wanted to cover the state in data centers. Those plans aren’t looking good now that Abbott is out and Hinojoa is in.

Musk broke his election day posting silence a little after 1 am. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he said on X. Chased off the land by its people, the billionaire looks to the sky.
a7719ef45c037686: After being defeated in the elections, the senator fled to the US with his family
Originally published on Global Voices
Art by Global Voices with Canva Pro. Photo by the Brazilian Senate. Fair use.

Forty-eight hours after losing the runoff in Brazil to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Flávio Bolsonaro, former president Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, a senator representing Rio de Janeiro, fled to the United States. From there, where his brother Eduardo, a former congressman, has lived since February 2025, he continues to challenge the results of the election he lost by 4.4 million votes, as attested by the Electoral Court (TSE), the Organization of American States (OAS), and other right-led governments in the region.

Upon landing in Miami, Flávio published a letter proclaiming himself “the true president of Brazil” and “president-elect of Brazil.” After 22 minutes — and a demand from the US Department of State — he retracted to “the leader of Brazil.”

US President Donald Trump had said that Brazil’s elections “looked rigged,” but he wouldn't “get involved.” The New York Times reported, however, that Flávio was helped by Trump's aides. “The jet [he traveled on] had been arranged by a White House official,” affirmed the newspaper.

Flávio’s narrative is that he is being persecuted by the Brazilian justice system and Lula’s government as an opposition leader, since the Supreme Court ordered the seizure of his passports — he also has Italian citizenship — right after his defeat was announced.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes, considered a foe of the Bolsonaro family and himself under suspicion for having links to the same disgraced banker connected to Flávio, issued the order in response to a Federal Police request that considered Flávio a flight risk. In Brazil, a president cannot be investigated for alleged crimes committed before their term, meaning that once elected, all pending investigations involving Flávio would have been suspended. This is also the first time in 24 years that Flávio will not have a seat to ensure his parliamentary immunity.

According to the Brazilian Federal Police, three elements indicated a flight risk in Flávio’s case: an interview his brother Eduardo gave to a podcast in the US defending the idea of him leaving the country, on October 23, his considerable economic power, and well-established structures abroad that could support him in a long stay.

The day after the election, after visiting his father, who is under house arrest convicted for a coup attempt, Flávio recorded a video complaining about the measure, claiming “he never thought about leaving the country” and promising to stay and answer to investigations. Overnight, apparently, he had a change of heart in time for a new plan.

Investigations and corruption suspicions have long surrounded his name. In 2020, Sergio Moro, the judge who convicted Lula, resigned as Bolsonaro’s justice minister, accusing the president of trying to intervene with the Federal Police to protect Flávio in an embezzlement and money-laundering inquiry. In a cabinet meeting, then-president Bolsonaro shouted at his ministers: “I won’t wait until they fuck my entire family,” saying he would fire whoever got in their way.

During this election campaign, skeletons in Flávio's closet were further exposed in stories published by the Brazilian press. Global Voices gathered the main ones here. Flávio is currently under three investigations at the Supreme Court.
Rachadinha

This is the case that led Jair Bolsonaro to allegedly interfere in the Federal Police in 2020. Flávio was indicted by Rio’s Public Prosecution Office for embezzlement, money laundering, and criminal organization. The case was later adjourned. Rachadinha (“split” in English) is a salary kickback scheme in which a politician hires someone for a certain position and then reclaims part of their salary.

In 2018, after Bolsonaro’s election, a report by the Council for Financial Activities Control (Coaf) pointed to atypical financial movements in the account of Flávio’s aide, Fabricio Queiroz, an old friend of his father. Queiroz, who was filmed paying for Flávio's daughters’ tuition in cash, was identified as the scheme’s operator. For the Public Prosecution Office, according to UOL news outlet, the scheme was used to cover Flávio’s personal expenses and to increase his patrimony.

There were also suspicions that a chocolate franchise shop, owned by Flávio, was used for money laundering. The investigation found 1,512 cash deposits in repeated amounts between March 2015 and December 2018 at the establishment.

An audio recording found by police in 2024 shows then-president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s attorneys, and Alexandre Ramagem, former director of the Brazilian Intelligence Agency (Abin), currently a fugitive living in the US, allegedly discussing a plan to free Flávio from the investigations through Federal Revenue Service employees.
‘Dark Horse’ and Vorcaro

On May 13, 2026, The Intercept Brasil published a story and an audio recording showing that the movie “Dark Horse,” a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro, starring Jim Caviezel, could have been financed by disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro. Before the story went out, a reporter from the news outlet asked Flávio about the case. The senator laughed and dismissed the question, saying: “That’s a lie! Where did you get this from?”

Vorcaro is at the center of one of the country's biggest scandals, involving politicians, members of the Supreme Court and other judges, and celebrities, through his bank, Master — its license was approved during Jair Bolsonaro’s government. Vorcaro is investigated for a fraud scheme that caused a BRL 47 billion (around USD 8.7 billion) loss to the Credit Guarantee Fund (FGC), which backs Brazil's banking system.

The messages published by The Intercept show Flávio negotiating with Vorcaro on WhatsApp. Flávio asked for BRL 134 million (USD 24.9 million) and received at least BRL 61 million (USD 11.17 million). In one of the last messages between them, before Vorcaro was arrested while trying to flee the country, Flávio tells him: “Brother, I am and will always be with you; there is no half-talk between us,” reported TIB.
Since he couldn’t deny their link, Flávio has repeated that the money he negotiated with Vorcaro was “private money for a private movie.”

This is also one of the investigations into Flávio at the Federal Supreme Court (STF), which targets the movie’s financing operation. Despite the movie being filmed in Brazil, Vorcaro sent the money to a fund in the US (Havengate), managed by a friend of Eduardo Bolsonaro’s. The final destination for the money hasn't been confirmed yet.
Willer Thomaz, a friend

Another inquiry investigates Flávio for money laundering and currency evasion, along with his friend Willer Tomaz, a Brazilian lawyer also currently in the US. Tomaz is under investigation for money laundering through betting companies and involvement in another scandal, a fraud scheme at the national pension fund (INSS).
Documents accessed by Brazilian news outlets showed that Tomaz alone moved BRL 5 billion (around USD 930 million) in betting sites and cashed out BRL 200 million (USD 37.2 million).

When Piauí magazine revealed that Flávio had travelled in Vorcaro’s plane with his family, the senator’s first reaction was to say that “fortunately, it was Willer's.” His friend shared the plane’s quotas with a Vorcaro company. Tomaz denied ever meeting with the banker.

In October, O Globo newspaper published that Flávio had been registered as a “master user” on an offshore account under the name of a company managed by Tomaz and registered on Madeira Island, Portugal. This status could give him “significant operational access,” according to the Federal Police. Piauí magazine also says the senator could have been an indirect partner in a betting company based in São Paulo, but controlled by another company registered in Madeira, also linked to Tomaz. Flávio denies it.

Folha de S. Paulo newspaper says that the relationship between Flávio and Tomaz began in 2019. During the COVID-19 parliamentary inquiry commission at the National Congress, two years later, the senator defended Tomaz, calling him a friend. They always denied being business associates, claiming they were only friends.
Ana Clara’s death and the militias

On the morning of February 2, 2021, five-year-old Ana Clara Machado was shot and killed while playing at the doorstep of her home, in Rio de Janeiro. The Military Police denied any confrontation or the presence of narcos in the area where their operation was taking place. Later, the Civil Police identified police officer Bruno Delaroli as the shooter and arrested him. In March, 2026, ICL Notícias, a news website, reported that Flávio Bolsonaro worked on the officer's defense team in the higher courts, trying to avoid a jury trial. Another news outlet, UOL, revealed he worked pro bono. Lula questioned the senator about his motives during a debate on TV Globo.
Also, according to ICL, this wasn’t the only case Flávio advocated for officers accused of killings. Folha says his career as a defense lawyer gained traction after he was elected senator.

During his political life, Flávio has had a long history of links to police officers identified as members of so-called militias — paramilitary groups mostly formed by active and retired officers, carrying out vigilante and organized crime activities in dominated territories. When a state deputy in Rio, Flávio employed at his office the mother and wife of Adriano da Nobrega, an ex-military policeman, linked to a militia known as Crime Office, whose main activities were to execute ordered killings. He also sent parliamentary money to an NGO connected to another police officer involved in the murder of Rio’s city councillor Marielle Franco. According to Piauí magazine, the militia man known as “Peixe” (fish) referred to Flávio as “our senator.”
ICL News says the UN will examine Flávio's links to the militias when analyzing Ana Clara’s case.
Written by Global Voices Brazil
6bee7ce701b5e0fa: On-premises high-performance compute (HPC) is still in demand, according to Hyperion Research, which estimates the market is expanding at almost 20 percent year-on-year, often driven by requirements for AI processing.
What Hyperion calls the "on-premises HPC and AI-for-Science" server market showed significant growth in the first half of 2026, with revenues hitting $16.5 billion, up 19.9 percent.

However, the analyst says unit shipments over the same period grew only 4.4 percent, meaning that systems are carrying a higher price tag due to greater use of costly components such as GPUs and other accelerators, not to mention the effects of higher memory costs, which have tripled or quadrupled since last year.

Its tracking of the HPC market is based on multiple surveys conducted of both buyers and suppliers, the firm says. The latest data shows a major change in the overall HPC market growth, heavily driven by a combination of the use of AI, large language models (LLMs), and purchases of large GPU/accelerator-based systems.

This trend was noted a couple of years ago, with Omdia reporting in 2024 that revenue growth from server sales was racing ahead of actual units shipped, as customers prioritized investment in highly configured server clusters for AI.

Much of that spending was by hyperscalers and cloud providers, seeking to profit from selling AI services to enterprise customers, but Hyperion’s figures focus on on-prem shipments, showing that many enterprises prefer to do their processing in-house.

According to Hyperion, Dell has now surpassed HPE as the biggest HPC vendor, with server revenues of $4.2 billion for the first half of 2026. HPE, which picked up supercomputing specialist Cray for $1.3 billion in 2019, had long been pack leader in the global HPC arena in terms of market share and revenue.

The figures put Dell on a 24 percent share, while HPE is not far behind on 21 percent. Lenovo and China-based Sugon trail behind at 4 percent share each, while 45 percent of the market is just labelled as "others" by Hyperion. This includes names such as Bull, which re-emerged from the shadows of Atos this year, plus Supermicro, Penguin Computing, and NEC.

The HPC infrastructure market is inherently cyclical. HPE recognized significant revenue in 2025 with sales of multiple exascale-class leadership machines, but procurement of that scale is intermittent and doesn't necessarily come along every year, Hyperion notes.

"Organizations and institutions are continuing to invest in their advanced computing infrastructure due to both replacing aging machines and the desire to adopt AI into their workflows to support their businesses and missions," said Hyperion Research CEO Earl Joseph.
"The growth reflects both a nominal increase in units being purchased and significant increases in system prices."
HPC systems are considered the backbone for many AI and AI-related applications, which has driven the overall HPC market to a new growth level, Joseph added. ®

74ed475c846c9cfc: I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.

While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level.

Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans.Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before.

What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second

Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto.

So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election.

There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process.

The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump.

With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees. Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments. Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations.

Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action. Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years. The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout.

Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry. According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers. And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development. Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4.

And AI critics fared well in their races, too. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly.

We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election. But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change. We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us.

a4ea24d5e823c74d: As first reported by The Register, VMware has returned to the low-end server virtualization market with a product called "vSphere Express."

The product will run on up to 128 processor cores and includes vMotion to allow live migration of VMs, automated restart of failed VMs, a distributed switch, rapid non-disruptive patching, and support for physical and virtual trusted platform modules.

"We have been listening to the market at the low end, and they want a basic core server virtualization platform," said Prashanth Shenoy, vice president of product marketing in Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF). He explained that each instance of vSphere Express will be discrete, meaning it won't be possible to manage them centrally.

"This is tested for small implementations," he told The Register. "We do not want a customer to run this on thousands of cores." Shenoy said the vSphere Foundation (VVF) enterprise virtualization product, and Cloud Foundation (VCF) private cloud suite, are appropriate for users with more complex needs. vSphere Express will, however, match the release cadence of VVF and VCF.
Under Broadcom’s ownership, VMware has enormously reduced the number of resellers in its channel program, meaning it no longer has partners who are a good fit for this product.

The virtualization giant will therefore sell vSphere Express through its distributors, most of which now operate cloud marketplaces at which affiliated resellers can acquire software – an arrangement channel folk call "two tier distribution."
We asked VMware to tell us the price it will charge for vSphere Express.

A spokesperson told us it will offer a per-core subscription license at a price "significantly lower" than VVF or VCF but declined to quote a dollar amount. "We encourage interested customers to reach out to their local reseller for information related to pricing and subscription terms," the spokesperson wrote.

VMware has also bulked out VVF and VCF a little, by adding disaster recovery and policy-based networking for virtual private clouds that it previously sold as add-ons. Shenoy pitched the additions as demonstrating VMware's intention to add value to VVF and VCF, in part by ensuring the bundles include tools that users are likely to consider represent essential functionality.

The Broadcom business unit will also add new features, such as native AWS S3-compatible object storage for its VSAN virtual storage. That update, due in calendar Q1 of 2027, means VSAN will become a more convenient platform on which to store the unstructured data that AI workloads rely on, therefore boosting the utility of VMware's AI Factory.
VMware also plans to make its AI Factory easier to implement.
"The idea is to focus more on AI, less on setup," Shenoy said.
Analysis: A welcome low-end return faces an uncertain reception

VMware's return to the low-end server virtualization market may not be well-received, because it has largely ignored users of its existing low-end vSphere Standard product for the last few years, and irritated many by insisting they upgrade to the more expensive and complex VCF.
The virtualization giant also cast aside thousands of resellers.
When The Register chats with members of the VMware community, we often hear that trust in the vendor has diminished.
Your correspondent therefore feels that vSphere Express will get a mixed reception.
Many vSphere Standard users will welcome a more appropriate and affordable upgrade option, especially as it means they won't need to learn new skills.
Other users and former partners will wonder if, having been bitten by Broadcom once, they should now be a little shy of vSphere Express.

Broadcom shareholders should be enthusiastic, as VMware's decision not to sell to the low end of the market blocked its onramp to new users. The chips 'n' code shop now has another way to get VMware growing, if it can restore trust. ®

1ff2567b9abdb34e: 250 House seats, ~55 Senate seats.
The past few months have been fascinating, watching pundits wrestle with what would become a historic election.

All presidents lose Congressional seats in the midterms (with only 4 exceptions). Given how close the margins had been, a shift in at least the House was likely. But this particular president has been uniquely polarizing. He won in 2024 by broadening traditional Republican demographics, adding a coalition that included young males, the uneducated, and Hispanics. That left the GOP coalition vulnerable in a normal midterm. How did that it turn out?
Everywhere I looked – stock futures, prediction markets, polls – turned out to be a panoply of errors.

Stock futures were in a deep selloff by 6 p.m.; prediction markets underpriced Democratic candidates; and the Polls, which got the general direction of the race right, had significant errors in the magnitude of the changes and wildly misread Democratic wins in traditionally GOP strongholds.
The S&P sold off about 100 points; now it’s up 150 points from those lows. At ~noon today we are +3% on the Dow and +2% on the SPX and NDX; that’s quite a swing.
maybe double-check your math…?
About those Prediction Markets:
The FT reported that “Polymarket’s gamblers had a bad night of forecasting, undermining the reputation of prediction markets.” (I have been criticizing their inaccuracy forever).
And the Polls!

The margins were far wider than even the final polls suggested; polling missed the “Texas Shock” where Talarico won a Senate seat by ~10 points and over a million votes; Gina Hinojosa won the Texas Governor’s race by 7% and 750k votes; traditional red states like Kansas and South Carolina elected Democratic senators for the first time in nearly a century. The so-called “Shy Trump” voter vanished; exit polls said 43% of voters cast ballots to oppose Trump vs 16% who supported him. Turnout Models missed intense motivation among Dem-leaning voters.

Some right-wing politicians imagined the MAGA coalition would last, but it showed signs of fraying almost immediately after the 2024 election. Each of the president’s three signature policies was a factor in the coalition pieces I mentioned to start: 1) ICE‘s aggressive immigration enforcement; 2) War, and a muscular foreign policy supporting multiple wars; 3) Inflation, driven partly by a silly tariff policy.

Whenever I channel William Goldman to emphasize how little we know about the future, I feel I am cheating, taking advantage of a flaw in the human condition that most either don’t know or don’t care about. We evolved in a very specific environment to deal with threats very different from the ones we face today.

Tribalism, a bad information diet, and an inability to accurately assess our own skill sets are a poor tool set when analyzing social events and politics. It is an utterly fatal combination when putting capital to work in markets…

e41fa079c65b5b9e: WASHINGTON: Donald Trump faced a radically transformed and hostile political landscape on Wednesday after US voters handed control of Congress to the Democrats in a stunning rebuke to his presidency.

The result was a personal humiliation for the 80-year-old Trump as a Democratic wave swept into his Republican heartland, boosted by anger at soaring energy costs and his costly, dragging war with Iran.

The Democratic capture of both the Senate and the House of Representatives signals an end to Trump's stranglehold on US politics and gives Democrats the power to block legislation, launch investigations into Trump's administration and thwart his appointments.

The results reflected deep frustration over the cost of living, tariffs and Trump's war with Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president.
"This is so incredibly exciting. We can get our country back," Kathy Jackoway said in Texas, celebrating a win by Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.
Trump struck a conciliatory tone despite his history of rejecting election defeats, telling The New York Times he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.
"I think the Democrats did a good job," the 80-year-old told Fox News, in rare praise for his political opponents. "They fought hard".
However, he sought to distance himself from his party's poor showing, adding: "I don't view it as a hit on me".
He acknowledged that the Iran conflict had contributed to the result but defended the military campaign, and he suggested the rival parties could find common ground on immigration.
Republican heartland
Democrats flipped seats that had long been held by Republicans, scoring breakthroughs in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine.
In Maine, former logger Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins.
In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the reliably conservative state since 1932.
Iowa had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008.
In Texas, Democrats won not only a Senate seat but also the governor's race, ending decades of Republican rule.
Democrats protected key Senate seats of their own, including Jon Ossoff in Georgia and an open seat in New Hampshire.
In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, making him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.
El-Sayed won despite a last-minute curveball when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers.
In the House, Democrats made gains in Pennsylvania, Kentucky, Arizona, North Carolina, Wisconsin and New Jersey, including districts Trump had carried comfortably in 2024.
Democrats also won Georgia's governorship, electing former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms as the first Black woman governor in US history.
Republicans had some consolation in Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds became the state's first Black governor and Ashley Moody retained a Senate seat.
However, the night was "a big wipeout and a strong repudiation of Donald Trump and his policies," George Washington University professor Todd Belt told AFP.
Trump on defensive
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump's MAGA movement "on the run".
Jeffries could become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January.

Trump insisted on social media that Republicans would have won "IN A LANDSLIDE" if he had been running, though he had repeatedly urged supporters throughout the campaign to "pretend I'm on the ballot".
He also repeated his threat to use the presidential veto on Democrat-passed bills, posting a picture on social media of a red baseball cap reading just: "VETO".
On the international front, Russia said it hoped Trump will continue his "peacemaking efforts" and China said it would "continue working" with the US.
Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he did not expect the election results to bring about a shift in US policy.
