12a079f968a979d1: JAKARTA: Indonesia's president sacked his chief of staff on Wednesday after his arrest in a wiretapping scandal that the government said pointed to treason, as the military said thousands of troops were being mobilised in the capital to boost security.

Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who was appointed chief of staff just a few weeks ago, was among three senior police officers detained on Tuesday accused of illegally tapping the phones of president Prabowo Subianto and unnamed journalists, politicians, government officials and business people since early 2025.
The illegal wiretaps were carried out by "rogue individuals" whose actions indicated treason, presidential spokesman Prasetyo Hadi said.
"It also tends toward acts that endanger state interests and the safety of the nation's leadership, including the safety of the head of state," Hadi told reporters.
Reuters could not immediately contact the three suspects or their lawyers.

The scandal comes as the president, a retired army general, faces pressure on multiple fronts, with widening public discontent about his big-spending populist policies and a slump in investor confidence over his administration's handling of the US$1.5 trillion G20 economy.

Political intrigue has been growing in Indonesia in recent weeks amid a rift between Prabowo and his two-term predecessor and former backer Joko Widodo, who remains highly influential, despite stepping back from politics.
Listyo, the former national police chief, was known as a loyalist of Widodo.
Military mobilised to 'safeguard and protect stability'
Troops were deployed to Jakarta to "safeguard and protect the stability of Indonesia's security," navy spokesman Tunggul said late on Wednesday.
The deployment was also related to upcoming training in areas near Jakarta, Tunggul, who goes by one name, added.
Soldiers on the capital's streets are not uncommon in Indonesia, where the military has been regularly deployed ahead of anti-government protests.

Elected president in 2024 by a big majority, former special forces commander Prabowo has seen his approval rating slide in his second year in office, with unease over food prices and his troubled free ​meals and village cooperatives programmes.

His administration has also been under intense investor scrutiny this year, with ratings outlook cuts, concerns about policy unpredictability, and record stock market routs after warnings by global index provider MSCI of an equities market downgrade.

Prabowo's party Gerindra said it would hold talks with other political parties to discuss the wiretapping, with its secretary-general Sugiono on Wednesday calling the scandal "insubordination" within the government.
In a post on X on Wednesday, former president Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono appealed to Prabowo to "restore civility to our politics".
Motive for wiretaps unclear
The government has yet to determine the motive for the wiretapping, said Yusril Ihza Mahendra, Indonesia's senior minister for legal affairs.
Police late on Tuesday said the suspects were being investigated for unauthorised wiretaps. The targets of the wiretaps were not disclosed.
Amnesty International in Indonesia urged authorities on Wednesday to reveal who the subjects of the wiretaps were and said the public had a right to know.
"If this scandal is allowed to continue unchecked, it could pave the way for a secret police apparatus used to tame the opposition," it said.

Sana Jaffrey, a state-building researcher at the Australian National University, said the troop deployment in Jakarta could signal concerns about tension between the military and police loyal to former chief Listyo.

"If Prabowo increasingly sees threats to his personal security, then this could strengthen the case for relying more heavily on the military," she said, adding that the immediate concern was the risk of unintended escalation.
1a7c02b0aaabbe64: He swore an allegiance to the US, but he was working for someone else. An IT specialist who worked across US government departments and held Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to transmitting sensitive documents to Ethiopia.
Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, admitted to the espionage offenses and agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months, the Justice Department confirmed on Tuesday.

A naturalized citizen of the US, Lemma, of Maryland, had worked for the US government in different capacities and across different teams, including for the National Reconnaissance Office, State Department (DoS), and Justice Department (DoJ), between 2019 and 2023.
These roles included working evening hours as an IT help desk technician at the DoS as of 2021, and daytime work at the DoJ as a contract management analyst, according to court documents.

Lemma had what's known as "downdraft" authority, which is to say that he was permitted to move classified files between classified systems, and unclassified files from classified to unclassified systems.

Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) – a secure workplace built for handling classified files.
The criminal complaint [PDF] initially stated that the alleged offending began in July 2022, although the DoJ more recently claimed that it began in 2021.
It claims Lemma was caught trawling "several" non-DoS classified portals and accessed intelligence reports without the proper authorization to do so.

On various occasions, Lemma, who had held Top Secret security clearance since 2020, copied information from at least 133 intelligence reports without need-to-know authorization, according to court documents.
Prosecutors claimed that the man downloaded more than 100 documents, burned them to CD/DVDs, and deleted their classification markings.

The material Lemma was copying was at the Secret and Top Secret levels, but burned onto discs with green labels, which are approved for employees and are supposed to signify the contents of the discs relating to unclassified material only.
Lemma would allegedly take these discs at the end of his shift and exit the SCIF with them tucked into his jacket pocket.

On other occasions, he was observed looking at classified material on his PC, then taking handwritten notes before folding the paper and again storing it in his pocket. This continued until around August 2023.
Prosecutors claimed that Lemma began transmitting information to Ethiopian officials via an encrypted messaging app in or around August and September 2022, weeks after the alleged offending began.

The files included documents, photographs, notes, maps, and information relating to Ethiopia, and officials would ask Lemma to provide details about command centers, logistics centers, military compounds, and other matters.

Communications also covered geopolitical topics, referencing "situations" in an unspecified African country that shares a border with Ethiopia to gain an advantage, and rebel groups involved in conflict with Ethiopia.
Lemma's messages also included encouragement to take action against paramilitary groups that were in conflict with Ethiopia on multiple occasions, say prosecutors.

According to the complaint, one of Lemma's messages said: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia." Later that day, on December 18, 2021, he wrote: "Please send dro[nes]," after sharing additional information.
Announcing the guilty plea on Tuesday, the Justice Department said many of Lemma’s contacts were senior Ethiopian officials across political, military, and intelligence branches of the government.

Lemma was also accused of storing copies of classified files on his own storage drives, which prosecutors claim were accessed remotely by Ethiopian officials numerous times between April and June 2023.
The man was additionally caught making several bank deposits exceeding $66,000 throughout the time he was working on behalf of foreign officials.
On one occasion, he was observed "angrily discouraging" bank staff from filing a currency transaction report after trying to deposit a sum greater than $10,000.

"Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.

"By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States." ®
1ecf5e8101ac2642: LONDON: A UK man accused of raping a woman whose husband invited strangers to have sex with her told a court Wednesday he heard her snoring but thought she was "roleplaying."

Richard Wilkins, 62, has pleaded not guilty to rape and assault by penetration in 2016, when he responded to a Craigslist ad by Philip Young to have sex with his then-wife Joanne, who has waived her right to anonymity.
Wilkins and three other men are standing trial at a court in southern England accused of various sexual offences committed jointly with the husband against Joanne Young.
Another man has also admitted similar charges.
Young has admitted multiple counts of drugging and raping her over 13 years.
The court was told he invited men to have sex with her while she was asleep or unconscious, presenting it as a "kink" for the couple.
Wilkins told Winchester Crown Court that he heard a "snoring noise" when he approached a blindfolded and bound Joanne Young in bed.
"I considered this was still part of the role-playing scenario that I was acting out," Wilkins said, adding she stopped snoring when he started having sex with her.
He said he did not suspect that she was drugged or drunk and did not know she was not consenting to the scenario.
Earlier this week, a jury heard statements from another defendant, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, who said Philip Young was a "vile monster" for his actions against his wife.
Sanderson-Doyle, who responded to a Craigslist ad when he was 21 in 2016, said he thought it was a couple who wanted to "fulfil our fantasy."
He said Young was "using pawns in his sick little game."
"I am not stupid and I am not a monster, in hindsight I should have done more," said Sanderson-Doyle, who denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching.
The other defendants are Norman Macksoni, 48, accused of rape, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, accused of sexual touching.
The prosecution argued that while the defendants may not have seen Young administer sedatives, they "could patently see its effect."
"They wanted to enact their fantasy and Phil Young's fantasy and they did not care about Jo Young's feelings at all," the prosecution previously told the jury.

There are multiple cases currently before UK courts of alleged drug-facilitated sexual assault, with awareness of the crime growing following the unrelated high-profile 2024 French trial of Dominique Pelicot.
He was found guilty of secretly drugging his wife, Gisele, for years and inviting scores of men to rape her while she was unconscious.
Gisele Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial to raise awareness about sexual violence.

410307eb478cd406: BUKIT MERTAJAM: Police arrested seven foreigners and seized suspected methylenedioxy methamphetamine (MDMA) powder and ketamine worth RM1.08 million during raids on two premises in Bukit Tengah here on Nov 1.

"Police arrested six men and a woman, all aged between 25 and 38. Inspections of both premises uncovered MDMA powder and ketamine valued at an estimated RM1.08 million," he said in a statement.

59942c90f7d9d522: WASHINGTON: As Republicans suffered a landslide defeat and Texas elected its first Democratic governor in more than three decades, one of the biggest losers of the US midterms was not on the ballot: billionaire Elon Musk.

The world's richest man spent nearly half a billion dollars to back Republican candidates and keep Texas red - a state home to his automaker Tesla, rocket-to-AI company SpaceX and a planned chipmaking venture between the two.

Those bets unravelled as Democrats seized both chambers of Congress and Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott in the Texas governor's race, in a stinging rebuke to US President Donald Trump, a close Musk ally whom the billionaire helped elect.
Musk, who urged his followers on X to vote Republican as recently as Tuesday, now faces a resurgent Democratic Party that he has spent years antagonising.
The GOP's largest donor even threatened retaliation last month on his social media platform after a report said Democrats were considering probes into his companies if they won midterms.
Shares of SpaceX fell 5.5 per cent, while Tesla was down 5.1 per cent as both stocks lagged the broader market.
One of Musk's biggest challenges could be slower approvals for the data centres crucial to tapping the US$28.5 trillion addressable market that SpaceX touted to investors ahead of its IPO.
Analysts and experts expect Democrats to tighten scrutiny of data-centre projects and push for construction moratoriums as local opposition grows over electricity costs.

"A Democratic sweep of Congress would put pressure on tech and potentially bring regulatory pressure on everything AI and possibly slow down the wild, wild west growth figures that we see daily and often take for granted," said Jake Dollarhide, CEO of Longbow Asset Management.

"Musk was the Hail Mary for Republicans leading down to the wire. Unfortunately, his large infusion of cash to back red states could not overcome higher utility bills, prices at the grocery store and prices at the gas pump."

Musk has also drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over restrictions on satellite communications used by Ukraine's military, mass federal job cuts under his watch at DOGE and the government contracts and subsidies flowing to his companies.
One of the lawmakers is Robert Garcia, the next House Oversight Committee chair, who had a blunt two-word message for Republicans and their allies on Tuesday evening: "Lawyer up."
In Texas, Musk also might have to deal with the tenuous relations between him and Hinojosa.
The incoming governor had sued to obtain emails between Musk and Abbott and accused the former governor of selling out the Lone Star state by offering favourable deals to the billionaire.

She has also dismissed Abbott's efforts to rein in data centres as political theater, calling instead for an immediate halt to new projects until lawmakers strengthened protections for local communities, as well as an end to tax breaks.

Musk himself appeared to make light of the hurdles. "Data centres in space looking pretty appealing right now," he posted on X, alluding to SpaceX's ambitious plan to put data centres in orbit despite major challenges around cooling and repairs.
The company's AI business is centred around Colossus and Colossus II, two of the world's largest AI data centres near Memphis.
Renting their computing power to customers including Anthropic has sent revenue soaring and helped SpaceX post its first profit as a public company.
But the company aims to nearly double capacity from 1.7 gigawatts at September-end to as much as three gigawatts by year-end, before scaling up to 13 gigawatts next year.
Any delays in bringing the capacity online may hamper Musk's ambitious revenue targets and intensify scrutiny from investors growing wary about AI infrastructure's mounting costs.
Chip research firm SemiAnalysis has identified more than nine gigawatts of planned or developing capacity, including new facilities at SpaceX's Starbase complex in Boca Chica, Texas.
That Boca Chica expansion could face resistance as Hinojosa has opposed the potential sale of a beachfront state park to SpaceX after Texas Monthly reported officials had discussed the deal.
"Let me be clear: Texas is not for sale," Hinojosa said last month.
Musk, meanwhile, has deleted his election-day appeal to his followers to vote Republican.

edf878584ccc74a4: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan's United States Senate race over former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, making him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.
"Michigan, we did it!" said El-Sayed in a speech attended by hundreds of supporters who screamed and hugged each other at his election headquarters in Detroit.
"I am so proud and honoured to stand here as your senator-elect from the great state of Michigan."
El-Sayed won despite a last-minute curve ball in his campaign when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers at the 11th hour.
The Michigan medical administrator rallied voters on leftist campaign promises, including universal healthcare, to win a key Senate seat for Democrats, taking over from the retiring Gary Peters.
El-Sayed held a nearly six-point lead on Rogers when networks called the race.
"We are sick and tired of being sick and tired. And I'm so proud of all the work.

"It was boots on the ground. We were always out, but we were never outworked," said party-goer entrepreneur Trunetta Roach, 75, who attended El-Sayed's victory party in downtown Detroit wearing US flag-design diamante high-heels.
"I'm feeling elated. The kids are all right. I was concerned about them. They didn't seem very engaged, but I was wrong. They showed up."
Republicans ran a scorched-earth campaign to paint Democrats as communists and branded El-Sayed a terrorist who would endanger Americans.
But the straight-talking 42-year-old El-Sayed pledged to help cash-strapped voters navigate America's fractured, for-profit healthcare system.
"You deserve to be able to see a doctor without getting a huge bill," he told Michiganders on the eve of the vote, vowing to upend America's divisive multibillion-dollar for-profit medical system.
During the race, El-Sayed drew huge campaign crowds across the state, even in deeply conservative Republican areas.
El-Sayed also vowed to get "money out of politics" and address the harsh economic woes that have voters yearning for a political newcomer to shake up the status quo.
The victory made El-Sayed the first Democratic doctor in the Senate since 1969.

"Everybody in politics is so trash. So to see ethical Muslims be at the forefront representing us and showing everybody what we're actually about... it means everything," said micro-influencer Maryam Bozai, 28.

At the victory party, crowds gathered around TVs tuned to left-leaning cable news channel MS NOW, cheering jubilantly each time the Democrat's trademark blue flashed on screen to announce another race won by the party.
"Tsunami! Tsunami!" chanted Ondine Fortune, 64, a Democratic Party media planner.

El-Sayed supporters rubbed shoulders with left-leaning influencers and union activists, a group that lent El-Sayed their formidable campaign infrastructure to reach Michigan's large organised labour community.
Eboni Taylor, a vice-president at Higher Heights which promotes Black women seeking office, said El-Sayed had "gone places where I just would not expect to see him".
"What's most remarkable is that he's showing up in places that are not the usual prescription for the Democratic Party.
"He's going wherever the people want him to be," said Taylor between social media livestreams and celebratory dancing.
El-Sayed faced Islamophobic attacks and mockery for his Arabic name from President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance. But El-Sayed may yet have the last laugh.
Addressing the vice-president, El-Sayed said in his victory speech "you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January."
The writer is from AFP

cc3a4b5c88edec76: LONDON: Britain's highest court on Wednesday heard an appeal against a government ban on activist group Palestine Action, proscribed as a terrorist organisation, as police moved to arrest protestors outside.
The two-day hearing at the Supreme Court comes as the ban has failed to quell support for the pro-Palestinian group co-founded by Huda Ammori, leading to mass arrests across the UK.
Multiple protesters carrying signs supporting Palestine Action - prohibited under terrorism laws - were arrested by police on Wednesday.
More than 300 supporters were detained at protests at the weekend.

According to campaign group Defend Our Juries, which has organised demonstrations backing the movement, around 4,200 people have been arrested since the British government outlawed Palestine Action in July last year.
Those detained include large numbers of pensioners, among them a priest, a former financial adviser, a military veteran and Swedish student climate activist Greta Thunberg.
Public support for Palestine Action is a criminal offence as the ban places the group in the same legal category as the Islamist Al-Qaeda organisation and Lebanon's Iran-backed Hezbollah.

The ban followed a series of acts of vandalism linked to the movement, including a trail of damage at a Royal Air Force base and actions targeting Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems in August 2024.
It was imposed under the UK's Terrorism Act and made membership of or support for the pro-Palestinian group a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
Ammori's lawyer Raza Husain told the court that out of 385 actions undertaken by the group in the last five years, "only three passed the terrorism threshold".
"Palestine Action fall within the tradition of a direct action protest group motivated by conscience," Husain said. The group has "never advocated for violence against the persons", she added.
In February, London's High Court dealt a blow to the government, ruling the decision to proscribe Palestine Action was "disproportionate".
The court found the ban had resulted in "substantial interference" with the rights of freedom of expression and assembly.
However, the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in June, concluding the ban was "not unlawful" and that Palestine Action was "a covert organisation operating with secret cells".
The appeal ruling added that it was "a fundamental mistake to overlook the fact that Palestine Action overtly promotes unlawful violence amounting to terrorism".
'Direct action'
Founded in 2020, Palestine Action describes itself as "a direct action movement committed to ending global support for Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime".
The organisation gained prominence after the outbreak of the Gaza war, triggered by Hamas's unprecedented attack on Israel on Oct 7, 2023.
Ammori has been granted permission to challenge the ban at the UK's highest court on a narrow procedural ground, arguing the Home Office failed to follow its own criteria in its decision.
If unsuccessful, Ammori has indicated she will take the case to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR).
The Home Office is set to reject the characterisation of the group as "non-violent", according to court documents.
Prominent Jewish groups also said in written submissions supporting the government that the Jewish community was "especially vulnerable to Palestine Action's violent activities".
The impact of the proscription has extended beyond the protest movement.
Books by bestselling Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who announced last year that she intended to donate part of her royalty income to Palestine Action, are no longer distributed in Britain.
This month, her British publisher Faber said it could no longer legally transfer UK-generated revenues to Rooney and therefore would cease distributing her books in the country.
6d4f9a6d25452a4c: WASHINGTON: Donald Trump faced a radically transformed and hostile political landscape on Wednesday after US voters handed control of Congress to the Democrats in a stunning rebuke to his presidency.

The result was a personal humiliation for the 80-year-old Trump as a Democratic wave swept into his Republican heartland, boosted by anger at soaring energy costs and his costly, dragging war with Iran.

The Democratic capture of both the Senate and the House of Representatives signals an end to Trump's stranglehold on US politics and gives Democrats the power to block legislation, launch investigations into Trump's administration and thwart his appointments.

The results reflected deep frustration over the cost of living, tariffs and Trump's war with Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president.
"This is so incredibly exciting. We can get our country back," Kathy Jackoway said in Texas, celebrating a win by Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.
Trump struck a conciliatory tone despite his history of rejecting election defeats, telling The New York Times he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.
"I think the Democrats did a good job," the 80-year-old told Fox News, in rare praise for his political opponents. "They fought hard."
But he sought to distance himself from his party's poor showing, adding: "I don't view it as a hit on me."
He acknowledged that the Iran conflict had contributed to the result but defended the military campaign, and he suggested the rival parties could find common ground on immigration.
Republican heartland
Democrats flipped seats that had long been held by Republicans, scoring breakthroughs in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine.
In Maine, former logger Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins.
In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the reliably conservative state since 1932.
Iowa had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008.
In Texas, Democrats won not only a Senate seat but also the governor's race, ending decades of Republican rule.
Democrats protected key Senate seats of their own, including Jon Ossoff in Georgia and an open seat in New Hampshire.
In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, making him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.
El-Sayed won despite a last-minute curveball when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers.
In the House, Democrats made gains in Pennsylvania, Kentucky, Arizona, North Carolina, Wisconsin and New Jersey, including districts Trump had carried comfortably in 2024.
Democrats also won Georgia's governorship, electing former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms as the first Black woman governor in US history.
Republicans had some consolation in Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds became the state's first Black governor and Ashley Moody retained a Senate seat.
But the night was "a big wipeout and a strong repudiation of Donald Trump and his policies," George Washington University professor Todd Belt told AFP.
Trump on defensive
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump's MAGA movement "on the run."
Jeffries could become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January.

Trump insisted on social media that Republicans would have won "IN A LANDSLIDE" if he had been running, though he had repeatedly urged supporters throughout the campaign to "pretend I'm on the ballot."
He also repeated his threat to use the presidential veto on Democrat-passed bills, posting a picture on social media of a red baseball cap reading just: "VETO."
On the international front, Russia said it hoped Trump will continue his "peacemaking efforts" and China said it would "continue working" with the United States.
Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, however, said he did not expect the election results to bring about a shift in US policy.

6e315d377a7fd3e9: Donald Trump struck a surprisingly conciliatory tone after the Democratic sweep of the United States midterm elections rendered him a lame-duck president. How long that will last is anyone's guess.
From renewed military action against Iran to vetoing Democratic legislation, the volatile 80-year-old could still use his remaining powers to cause major disruption in his last two years in office.
"Every time Trump has been backed into a corner, he has shouted more and come out fighting," said Peter Loge, director of George Washington University's School of Media and Public Affairs.
VETOES AND EXECUTIVE POWER
Trump congratulated the Democrats on Tuesday and said he would be ready to work with them. He may have to, especially if Republicans turn on him over a defeat many of them blame on the Iran war.
But at the same time, Trump repeatedly boasted of his executive power to veto any Democratic legislation that crosses his desk in the Oval Office.
He even posted a picture of a red baseball cap with the word "VETO".
Trump's administration has reportedly drawn up a plan to use executive orders to push through his hardline immigration policies, much as he did in his first 100 days of his second term.
The twice-impeached Trump, the first convicted criminal ever to be elected president, has said he is also ready to fight back against Democratic-led investigations.
WAR WITH IRAN
Foreign policy is the one area in which lame-duck US presidents still have wide-ranging powers.
Trump may renew large-scale military operations against Iran, although he indicated on Tuesday that he was still seeking a deal to end the war he launched in February.
"Otherwise I'll just finish the job," he told Fox News.
"I don't think he wants his legacy to be a warmonger. He wants his legacy to have left America stronger," said Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution.
Trump also dismissed speculation that he could fire Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth as the Iran war drags on, as part of a cabinet reshuffle.
UKRAINE, DETENTE AND TRADE
Trump has long wanted to be seen as a peacemaker and is likely to continue to push Ukraine to agree to a settlement with Russia.
Fresh trilateral talks are set for next week.
But Trump's leverage with the leaders he views as his great power equals —Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin — may be hit by his midterms defeat.
The election hammering comes less than two weeks before the three could potentially meet at a summit in China later this month.
MONUMENTS TO HIMSELF
Trump may, however, choose to step back from confrontation and focus on his favourite subject — stamping his physical legacy on Washington.
In his closing midterms speech, Trump barely mentioned policy and instead talked about his renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other plans to beautify Washington.
His pride and joy is the giant US$400 million ballroom that he is building at the White House, and which is due to be completed in late 2028 — shortly before he leaves office for good.

dbc478cee2a8f476: In 2012, as the driver of deaths in the opioid crisis began moving from prescription pills to heroin, Laura Bohn was tasked with finding safer drugs to manage pain.

Funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, in 2017 she and other scientists revealed in the science journal Cell that several compounds—including a particularly promising one called SR-17018—could relieve pain in mice without causing respiratory depression. That’s a big deal, because respiratory depression is typically what causes people using opioids to stop breathing and die.

Bohn, senior associate vice president of research at University of South Florida Health, says her team filed a patent on SR-17018. db8c74c2da5dfb22: BANGKOK: Five Uyghurs detained in Thailand since 2014 are subject to Chinese arrest warrants, the kingdom's security chief said Wednesday, adding that a court would decide if they would be returned to China.
Human rights groups have raised concerns about the men – members of the Muslim minority group who activists say are persecuted in China – after two of them were pardoned by Thailand last month.
They were among more than 300 Uyghurs held in Thailand in 2014, most of whom have since left – including a group of around 40 sent last year to China, a move that sparked international outrage.
The five were jailed for trying to escape immigration detention in 2020 and under Thai law have to serve their sentences before deportation.
Two of them were pardoned last month and are in immigration detention awaiting their fate.
"These five have arrest warrants in China and they have no refugee status," Chaipruak Doungprapat, secretary-general of Thailand's National Security Council, told reporters on Wednesday.

It adds: "China is slandering us. We aren't terrorist(s)."
'RATHER DIE'
Thailand's foreign ministry did not immediately reply to emailed questions from AFP.
But a ministry official told a parliament committee on September 16 that both China and a Western country had requested five detained Uyghurs be sent to them, according to parliamentary minutes.
Kannavee Suebsang, chairman of Peace Rights Foundation, said defence lawyers have not been given access to the two pardoned men since October 21 when they were moved to immigration custody.
The pair told a Thai human rights commissioner on Wednesday that they want to be resettled in a third country, Kannavee told AFP.
"They refuse to return to China and would rather die first."

6b6933bafb9791d0: The 1993 Highland Towers tragedy claimed 48 lives. The incident prompted greater attention to regulations governing hillside development, slope maintenance and disaster-response coordination.

Recurring concerns surrounding hillside development in Penang serve as a reminder that the lessons of Highland Towers must never be forgotten. For four decades, residents and civil society groups have raised objections to high-density projects on the island's steep and environmentally sensitive slopes.
These concerns date back to the late 1980s and gained renewed prominence in 2007, when opposition mounted against the proposed RM25 billion Penang Global City Centre at the Penang Turf Club site.

Over the years, planning guidelines and restrictions have been introduced to address the challenges of hillside development, including provisions in the Penang Structure Plan relating to slopes above 76m or with gradients exceeding 25 degrees.
However, concerns have persisted, particularly over the balance between development needs and environmental and public safety considerations.
Penang has experienced several devastating landslides. In 2017, a landslide at the Granito construction site in Tanjung Bungah claimed 11 lives.

A year later, the Bukit Kukus landslide, during hill-clearing works, killed nine workers. The latest tragedy in Paya Terubong last month, which claimed the life of 73-year-old retired doctor Dr Wong Kar Lin, has once again brought these concerns into sharp focus.

Dr Wong was among those who voiced concerns about hillside development. Penang's limited supply of flat, developable land, coupled with strong demand for housing and infrastructure, has inevitably placed greater attention on alternative development sites.

Hillside land also presents different land acquisition and development cost considerations. These competing priorities make it all the more important that safety remains paramount at every stage of the planning and development process.

Following the latest tragedy, residents and civil society groups have called for a State Commission of Inquiry and a white paper to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident and identify lessons to be drawn.

A transparent and comprehensive examination would help address public concerns, establish responsibility and strengthen confidence in the processes governing hillside development. Penang's experience should serve as a reminder to other states.

Ultimately, planners, developers and the authorities must ensure every hillside project is supported by rigorous geological assessments, proper slope stabilisation measures and effective drainage systems.
These safeguards must continue beyond planning approval, with regular monitoring, maintenance and compliance throughout construction and after completion.

Economic progress is necessary, but it must never come at the expense of public safety, environmental sustainability or the quality of life of existing communities. The consequences of getting it wrong are simply too grave.
34c04ea0d4ee0112: PARIS: Alexander Zverev made a losing start to his reign as world number one on Wednesday as the two-time Grand Slam champion went down 7-6 (7/5), 6-2 to an inspired Lorenzo Musetti at the Paris Masters.

e7a718344062c08f: LONDON: Britain's centuries-old parliament is at risk of a "Notre Dame-like" fire or other catastrophe if lawmakers continue to put off a major restoration project, MPs warned Wednesday.
Crumbling masonry, ageing electrics, frequent leaks and high asbestos levels are some of the problems besetting the Palace of Westminster, parts of which are over 900 years old.
Billions of pounds are required to renovate the estate, which sits within a Unesco world heritage site, but parliamentarians have been unable to decide for years on how to proceed.
Parliament's public accounts committee said the delay was leading to spiralling costs and risked causing a "catastrophic failure" that would harm the UK's "morale and reputation."

"A lack of action risks, for instance, the chamber being plunged into darkness during the state opening of parliament," said chair Geoffrey Clifton-Brown MP, referencing when the monarch comes to the lower House of Commons to read out the government's legislation plans.
"Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building's roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life.
"These are not notional possibilities, but real and rising risks," he added.
Most of the central London site, including the internationally recognised Elizabeth Tower commonly known as Big Ben, was built during the 1800s when Queen Victoria was on the throne.
Parliamentarians first voted to move out of the central London site in 2018 to allow extensive repairs. But there has since been disagreement about whether this should go ahead.
A series of votes is expected in both the House of Commons and the upper House of Lords chamber on the so-called Restoration and Renewal programme later this year.
The current options include a "full decant" costing up to £15.6 billion and lasting up to 24 years, where both houses leave for much of the works.
A partial decant called "enhanced maintenance and improvement plus" where no more than 30 percent of staff would stay on site at any one time is projected to cost £39 billion and take up to 61 years.
Current timescales predict that work would start in 2032.
In its report, the committee warned that the weekly cost of maintenance on the parliamentary estate is expected to grow from the current £1.5 million to £2 million in coming years.
Each year the programme is delayed will add £420 million to the lifetime costs of delivering the scheme, it added.

c721d961b220bcac: HONG KONG: The WTA told AFP that protecting players is "a key priority" as former Australian Open champion Sofia Kenin and Britain's Katie Boulter on Wednesday became the latest women's tennis stars to be abused online.
Kenin lost in three sets to British teenager Mika Stojsavljevic at the Hong Kong Open and within minutes the American's Instagram page began receiving abusive and offensive messages.
Among the comments were references to the 27-year-old's appearance and remarks about her parents, much of it graphic and littered with swear words.
A comment from an account set to private and with no profile picture or followers wrote: "You're not even human. Do you realise how many families you've bankrupted around the world?".
The Women's Tennis Association (WTA) believes that there is clear evidence linking betting and some of the more serious abuse.
"Protecting players and the wider tennis family from online threats and abuse is a key priority for the WTA," said a spokesman.
Boulter last year spoke out about the scale of the online hate, including death threats, directed at her and other players.
"I think it just kind of shows how vulnerable we are," Boulter told the BBC, saying it was hard sometimes to work out what was a real-life threat and what wasn't.
The 30-year-old Boulter followed Kenin in being defeated in Hong Kong on Wednesday, with abuse starting to roll into her Instagram page even before her match with the American Claire Liu finished.
On Tuesday, Boulter's fellow Briton Jodie Burrage suffered a first-round exit at the Chennai Open in India.
The 27-year-old later shared a story on her Instagram page showing the abuse, including death threats, that she was sent in the aftermath.
Much of the abuse players get is through direct messages.
Germany's Eva Lys tagged the WTA from her Instagram handle and asked: "When will something be done?"
The WTA said it has given Burrage extra support, including on the ground in Chennai, while investigations are under way to identify those responsible.
Women tennis players were subjected to more than 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025, according to a report in July.
Among the steps that the WTA has taken along with other tennis bodies is the establishment in 2023 of an online monitoring service.
Through that system, abusers can be identified, investigated and in serious cases reported for prosecution.
Abusive comments can also be flagged for removal from the relevant websites, although social media platforms have been accused of not doing enough.

Our goal was to discover whether the way a company communicates with the public about its donations affects how much credit it gets from consumers for those gifts. Across seven studies, we found that companies earn more goodwill when they give consistently – say, US$20,000 a month – instead of making a single $240,000 gift. On average, consumers also said they were more likely to buy from those companies. To test this premise, we did two real-world studies. First, we partnered with GiftAMeal, a U.S. company that runs a free app for diners. Each time someone takes a photo of their meal at a participating restaurant and shares it on social media, GiftAMeal donates to a local food bank. We ran two versions of GiftAMeal’s Facebook ad, which together reached 67,576 people. One said the company “donated 25,000 meals every month” last year. The other said it “donated 300,000 meals” last year. Both were true, and everything else about the ads was the same. We found that people who saw the monthly version were about 21% more likely to click on the ad. Next, we worked with Salt + Smoke, a Midwestern barbecue restaurant. When we emailed 75,514 customers who subscribed to its newsletters, half read that the company would give $5,000 a month from September through December to a small, local charity that supports early childhood education programs. The other half read that it would make a one-time donation of $20,000. Subscribers who read about the monthly donation pledge were nearly twice as likely to click through to the restaurant’s website as those who read about the one-time gift pledge even though the total was the same. Then we ran online experiments with more than 7,400 people to learn why and when consistent giving makes people view a company more favorably. We found that, on average, when a company gives monthly, people see its charitable support as a more genuine commitment to the causes. Why it matters U.S. companies gave nearly $44 billion in 2025 alone. And this kind of giving is popular with the public. In a 2022 survey, 88% of Americans said it’s important for companies to make the world a better place. Companies frequently promote their donations with the largest numbers they can muster. For example, Microsoft announced that the software giant and its employees donated $256 million in 2025; Walmart and its foundation say they have donated $2 billion in 2026. Yet boasting about big numbers may not impress people as much as emphasizing the consistency of donations. This may help explain why companies often struggle to convey their charitable efforts in ways that win people over. Even if companies give only once a year, they can indicate that they are engaged in a steady pattern of giving. For example, they can make their annual gifts on Giving Tuesday every year. Donating on the same day or as part of the same fundraising campaign every year can signal an ongoing commitment, not a one-off. What still isn’t known We don’t yet know how long the reputational boost companies may get from recurring donations might last, or whether those donations can translate into long-term customer loyalty. It’s also possible that what we found would not apply during emergencies. For example, consumers might be happy to see a company make one big gift right after a hurricane when a local community’s needs are immense. What’s next Along with Park and Cynthia Cryder, a Washington University in St. Louis marketing professor, I’m now studying other ways that corporate philanthropy can affect how much credit companies get for doing good. So far, we’ve found that companies may earn less goodwill when they ask customers to chip in to their charitable campaigns. People seem to expect companies to carry more of the load themselves. The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work. 7130e166440992e2: Datacenter restrictions found broad support in this week's US midterm elections.

Data Center Watch, which tracks grassroots opposition to compute sheds across America, examined the public positions of 74 selected candidates across the 36 states that elected governors in the midterm elections on November 3.

It found that 43 percent of those candidates supported a ban or moratorium on new projects, while another 51 percent backed further regulation or conditional development. Only about 5 percent had no stated public position.
Support for bans or moratoriums crossed party lines, although it was more common among the Democratic candidates examined (60 percent) than Republicans (30 percent).
Candidates from both major parties backed restrictions in eight states: Maryland, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon, Wisconsin, and Texas.

Texas has experienced a boom in data campus development recently, thanks to its ample energy resources and light-touch regulations, although outgoing governor Greg Abbott ordered a pause earlier this year while audits of energy and water use were carried out. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who supports a temporary moratorium on datacenter buildouts and has vowed to "stop the data center takeover,” defeated Abbott in Tuesday's election and will take office in January.
These positions matter to developers because governors can shape state regulation, energy policy, and permitting, although approval powers vary by jurisdiction.
However, temporary pauses and targeted construction restrictions do not necessarily amount to opposition to all datacenter development.

Things were even starker where folks got to vote directly on the issue, with measures regarding datacenters appearing on the ballot as well as candidates. Data Centers on the Ballot, which tracked many of these, found that 43 out of 46 municipalities where tighter restrictions on server farms were up for a vote had approved those at the time of publication. Only in one case, the City of Harwood in North Dakota, had restrictions been rejected, and 2 had yet to post results.

AI-related campaign spending has also come under scrutiny. Guardrails Alliance, a labor-backed pressure group, described Leading the Future, a super PAC network opposing AI regulation, as "largely a non-factor" in the elections. It alleged the network avoided the most competitive races because "they know their money is politically toxic."
Anti-datacenter sentiment has grown in the US in response to the facilities popping up in people's backyards, often without them having any say in the process.

A Gallup survey earlier this year discovered that more than 70 percent of Americans would be against the construction of one in their neighborhood, while a Pew Research Center survey found that Americans increasingly believe datacenters are bad for the environment and blame them for rising household energy bills.

Pew also found that advertisers spent almost $12 million on Facebook and Instagram political ads mentioning datacenters between July 27 and October 24. Among those running in October through the study's cutoff, 57 percent opposed datacenters and just three percent supported them.
Common themes included corporate interests, energy use, environmental effects, and water consumption. ®

Find out how the sight-restoring implant works.

MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here

In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.
This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.

e267ae6c90c16d4d: KUALA LUMPUR: Singer and celebrity chef Datuk Fazley Yaakob has expressed his embarrassment over insensitive comments made by fellow celebrities regarding the religious celebrations of other faiths.

b3b8da2d5e15e20a: PARIS, Nov 4 — Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died on Tuesday as a result of injuries he suffered in a sickening collision with FC Andorra’s goalkeeper in a Spanish second division match.
The 30-year-old is sadly not a unique case of a player dying either on the pitch or because of an injury sustained during the match.
AFP Sport highlights five such fatalities:
Marc-Vivien Foe, June 2003
Cameroon midfielder Foe collapsed after a heart attack during a Confederations Cup semi-final against Colombia in Lyon, France.
The former Manchester City, West Ham and Lyon player was carried from the pitch as medical staff tried to revive him with mouth-to-mouth resuscitation and oxygen.
After trying to restart his heart for 45 minutes without success he was declared dead, aged just 28.

His death prompted improvements in both the testing of footballers for heart problems and the treatment they can receive during matches, including training club medical teams in CPR and using defibrillators.
Antonio Puerta, August 2007
Spain international Puerta, 22, collapsed while playing for Sevilla in a La Liga match against Getafe and died three days later from multiple organ failure stemming from prolonged cardiac arrest.
It was three months after he had helped Sevilla to win the Uefa Cup.
Spanish legend Sergio Ramos has a tattoo tribute to Puerta and wore a T-shirt dedicated to him as Spain won the 2010 World Cup.
“Antonio has always been with me. The next game, I went out on the field with his shirt and for a long time after that, I wore one that was dedicated to him,” said Ramos.
Phil O’Donnell, December 2007
The Motherwell captain died of heart failure towards the end of his side’s 5-3 Scottish Premier League win over Dundee United in December 2007.
The 35-year-old midfielder collapsed just as he was about to be substituted and was treated for around five minutes on the field before being taken to a waiting ambulance.
O’Donnell played for Scotland, Celtic and Sheffield Wednesday during his career and his death caused widespread grief in Scottish football, causing a number of fixtures to be postponed.
“He was a man among boys in every sense, in his attitude, his professionalism and integrity and sincerity,” his manager Mark McGhee said.
Cristiano Junior, August 2009

The 25-year-old Brazilian, who was then the highest paid footballer in India, collided with the opposing goalkeeper when he scored a goal for his club Dempo 12 minutes from time in the 2004 Federation Cup final in Bangalore.
Junior, who had moved to India to earn enough money to build a house for his mother back home, collapsed and was immediately attended to by his Nigerian strike partner Santi Martins.
Martins stayed with him until an ambulance whisked him off to hospital but he was pronounced dead on arrival having suffered cardiac arrest.

“The match continued. We played the remaining 12 minutes, received the trophy and were told of Cristiano’s death only when we reached the hospital. We broke down, unable to control ourselves,” his teammate and club captain Stanley Colaco told the Times of India in 2021.
Juan Izquierdo, August 2024
The 27-year-old Uruguayan central defender suffered cardiac arrhythmia during his club Nacional’s Copa Libertadores last 16 match with Brazilian outfit Sao Paulo FC.
Taken to hospital, he died five days later of “cardio respiratory arrest associated with his cardiac arrhythmia”.
His second child had only been born 10 days prior to his death. His club described his death as an “irreplaceable loss”. — AFP
fdef5dc16fde71c3: PARIS, Nov 4 — After thrilling the international festival circuit, US indie sensation Club Kid set in the queer New York party scene will hit cinemas this week ahead of what many critics see as a tilt at the Oscars.

The debut film from Jordan Firstman became one of the buzziest titles at this year’s Cannes Film Festival in May, leading to a bidding war among distributors that was won by US independent film giant A24.
It has since won awards at festivals, with expectations steadily built by a string of rave reviews that have handed the movie a rare 100-per cent rating on aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes.

Firstman, 35, told AFP in an interview ahead of the film’s international release from Wednesday that he had used his own personal experience of New York’s underground gay club scene for the movie that he also wrote and acts in.
“I know it deep in my bones, and I know the beauty of it, and I know the complications of it, and I know the pain of it, and so I wanted that all to just be shown,” he said in Paris.
The film chronicles the life of a gay New Yorker in his thirties, a queer drug-loving party promoter who suddenly discovers he is the father of a 10-year-old child.
It offers viewers an immersion into the underground LGBTQ party scene where everyone speaks the same coded language: “K” for ketamine, “C” for cocaine, “G” for GHB, “3” for 3-MMC.
Some scenes in the film are shot in real underground parties.

But while it could easily have gotten lost in a plea for same-sex parenting or in re-telling a story about addiction, Firstman instead focuses on the universal by telling the gentle yet chaotic story of learning how to be a parent.
“It’s a love story between a father and a son. It’s a love story about community. It’s a family love story about chosen family,” he explained.
His aim was to produce a queer re-telling of family-based classics such as The Kid by Charlie Chaplin or Academy Award Best Picture winner Kramer vs Kramer by Robert Benton.
Self-esteem
With a host of industry magazines and critics tipping the movie as a possible Oscars contender, Firstman says his hard-partying past is behind him as he deals with the bright glare of publicity.
“I can’t afford on a Monday to be hungover,” he joked.
Before making Club Kid, which features model Cara Delevingne as a cocaine-addled party organiser, he was best known for short queer comedy clips on Instagram.
While writing his first feature, he said he also wanted to explore the difficult journey to self-respect and love that many LGBTQ people have to take.
“If you grow up gay, people bully you or your family doesn’t accept it. I think a lot of people have this, and I think it doesn’t really get better unless you really, really work on it,” he told AFP.
Although he said he had “struggles with self-esteem”, he was supremely confident in his abilities as a writer and director.
“I almost had an inflated sense of self when it came to my work. When people didn’t want to make my movies or make my TV shows, I was like, ‘they’re the idiots, I’m right’,” he explained.
Club Kid takes place in 2016 — a year that Firstman now looks back on with nostalgia.
“There was just something that felt really fun and cool (in that year),” he said.
“Right after, Trump got elected in America, it has never for a day gotten better. The second we got rid of Trump, we got a pandemic. The second the pandemic ended, we got Trump again.
“2016 was the last good year, I think,” he said. — AFP
638925d1ac78f5ff: GENEVA, Nov 4 — The number of women in top leadership jobs at companies worldwide has risen since 2013, but inequalities remain at lower managerial levels, the International Labour Organization said Tuesday.
The share of companies with a female board chair surged from 13.1 per cent in 2013 to 30.9 per cent last year, the United Nations agency said in a report.
The share with a woman chief executive rose from 23.4 per cent to 28.2 per cent in the same period.
But the report found women remain under-represented in the corporate hierarchy overall, holding just 30.5 per cent of managerial positions globally — up from 24.5 per cent in 2000.

“Gender equality is a fundamental right, and the evidence is clear that it is also a powerful driver of sustainable enterprises and economic growth,” ILO Director-General Gilbert Houngbo said in a statement.
The report was based on a survey of 11,957 companies in 99 countries.
It found a “growing gap” between companies’ commitments on gender equality and implementation on the ground.

While nearly three-quarters of firms had a gender equality and diversity policy or equivalent measure in place in 2025, the share implementing such initiatives — such as maternity leave and equal pay programmes — fell from 37.4 per cent in 2018 to 26.5 per cent last year, it said.
“At a time when enterprises are competing for skills and talent, leaving women’s potential untapped makes little business sense,” said the ILO’s Maria Paz Anzorreguy.
“The evidence increasingly tells us what works. The priority now is to put it into practice and scale it.”
The report recommended bolstering leadership pipelines for women, using gender metrics and voluntary targets, and improving women’s access to roles where they remain under-represented.
It also called for “action to address structural barriers outside the workplace, including unequal care responsibilities, occupational segregation and persistent social norms”. — AFP
416b7eba9f32ddf4: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.

This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.

Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.

e61f909daa74cb73: Capita has repeatedly "broken" promises to resolve the "chaos" engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) following its takeover of the administration – a move that left thousands of retired public sector workers unpaid.

So says Parliamentary spending watchdog, the Public Accounts Committee, which this week launched an inquiry into the handover of the ten-year £239 million contract in December from previous incumbent MyCSP.

As The Register exclusively revealed, the troubles began early on as members of CSPS – which manages pensions for 1.7 million people – complained of unrecognized passwords and usernames on the portal Capita developed. Capita said it inherited 132,100 complex remediation cases, and claimed the work-in-progress backlog from the prior system was more than double the 37,000 items when it won the deal in 2023.

Capita ran to Microsoft for support, and promised the use AI and automation, in addition to its 500 full-time employees working on the project, would resolve the issues by March. It missed this deadline, as well as one set for June 30 and is set to miss March 2027.
The government subsequently withheld a £10 million payment to Capita over the CSPS fiasco.

The National Audit Office, a spending regulator, has already launched its own probe into the failures and is now joined by the PAC, which says thousands of civil servants and their families have struggled to on and collect their pensions

The PAC has already held three evidence sessions on Capita and the government’s efforts to ameliorate the situation. The law was changed in the Budget 2026 to mitigate the impact of administrative delays in CSPS on bereaved families.
Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair at the PAC, said in a statement:

"In response to the alarming reports of hard-working civil servants being thrown into financial uncertainty following Capita’s takeover of the CSPS, we have held a number of evidence sessions with both the top leadership of Capita, and the civil servants and ministers of the Cabinet Office who have ultimate responsibility for overseeing the contract.

"Over and over again, promises have been made and broken by Capita, to our faces in formal evidence sessions, that they will get a grip on what has gone wrong. As a result, we are launching an inquiry, which will be informed by the authoritative factual basis provided by the NAO, which supports the scrutiny work of this Committee."

The inquiry will draw on the finding of the NAO's forthcoming report on the switch of CSPS to Capita, and will take into consideration the status of the scheme at go-live date, how Capita has performed, and the effect on CSPS members, plus take a look into the way the Cabinet Office has overseen the prior scheme and the switch to Capita. ®

Updated to add at 1407 UTC: Capita has been in touch to say how "deeply sorry" it is about the "frustration" that the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme "has caused members and their families." It said it had "made progress," but had a lot more to do. It said its teams are working to resolve outstanding cases "as quickly as possible, with particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging personal circumstances."

e2ee971d671cdbf0: BRUSSELS, Nov 4 — There may be jubilation in Europe after a stunning rout of the Republicans in the US midterm elections left President Donald Trump weakened.
But there are no guarantees that the political earthquake will change key US policies.
Here are the areas Europeans will be watching for a shift:
Trump reined in?
After a rollercoaster of tariffs, trashing Ukraine, and threats to Greenland, diplomats in Brussels were welcoming the results.
“There is relief here that this is the beginning of the end of the Trump era and nobody is happier than Europeans,” one diplomat told AFP, granted anonymity like others to discuss the issue.
The first expectation appears that the Democratic victories could help rein in Trump and begin righting the ship — at least at home.
“Hope is that with checks and balances some confidence will come back in the US system,” said a second senior EU diplomat.
But there is also a clear sense that America’s inward turn under Trump is unlikely to halt.
“If anything, the US will turn even more inwards and focus on the domestic political fight between the White House and the Congress,” a third diplomat said.
Meanwhile on the international stage Trump should still have a freer hand — and get even more aggressive.
“Trump still has executive powers and has been ignoring Congress,” the same diplomat said.
Ukraine
Despite the caution, Europe dearly wants to see a shift in Washington’s approach to the war in Ukraine.
Ahead of the midterms, Trump yet again lashed out at Ukraine and cosied up to Russia as Washington has renewed its push to end the fighting.
The Democrat win will now usher in a more vocal pro-Kyiv majority in Congress that could pressure Trump to change tack.
But there is little hope that the United States will go back to being a major financial backer for Ukraine.
Officials in Brussels say they are focused on plugging a €70-billion (RM321 billion) hole in Kyiv’s finances next year.
And while they’re pushing other countries such as Britain, Canada and Japan to do more, they are certainly not counting on the United States.
Iran
As the impact of Trump’s Iran war continues to send inflation up in Europe, the continent is anxiously eyeing what happens next in the Middle East.
But with Washington carrying out fresh strikes in recent days, there are fears that the situation could escalate again now the midterms have passed.
Throw in as well the unpredictable situation in Israel, where Trump ally Benjamin Netanyahu is engaged in his own post-election horse-trading.
Troops
At Nato, Washington’s European allies are nervously waiting for the results of a Pentagon review of US forces on the continent that looks set to be unveiled in December.
Multiple diplomats have previously said they do not expect the midterms to impact the result.
Now with the Democrats threatening to go after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, one of the most aggressive voices on Europe could be under fire at the Pentagon.
Despite that, Europeans remain clear-eyed and insist they are not backing down on efforts to take more responsibility for their own security.
Tariffs
One of Europe’s major bugbears with Trump are the tariffs he’s imposed.
Getting him to backtrack on one of his centrepiece economic policies seems unlikely.
Democrats seeking to bring down inflation could try to roll back some of the measures.
But some look likely to stick around.
In a recent poll from the Washington-based Council on Foreign Relations, only one quarter of Americans backed removing all the tariffs on the EU.
Digital
Another area of conflict has been Trump’s opposition to the EU efforts to curb big tech.
Now with the Democrats pledging to crack down on the power of Silicon valley — Europe is hoping it won’t face such strong headwinds.
“We will not change our enforcement of our digital rules, and we don’t expect changes on such issues with the White House,” an EU official told AFP.
“But we expect more room to discuss, to cooperate with Congress on global shared challenges” such as AI and cyber security. — AFP

9bd07b49241958e4: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 4 — The retail price of RON97 has dropped by 20 sen to RM4.70 per liter, while unsubsidised RON95 and diesel have both dropped 15 sen to RM4.27 and RM5.12 per liter respectively for the period of November 5 to 11.

The Ministry of Finance (MOF), in a statement today, announced that this pricing is determined based on the Automatic Pricing Mechanism (APM) formula, compared to the current prices of RM4.90 for RON97, RM4.42 for unsubsidised RON95, and RM5.27 for unsubsidised diesel.

“The regional petroleum market shows signs of moderation following an increase in the supply of refined fuels, including petrol and diesel stocks in Singapore, which serves as one of the market references for petroleum pricing in Malaysia.

“This development, together with the drop in Brent crude oil prices at the end of the Automatic Pricing Mechanism (APM) calculation period, indicates the possibility of lower price pressures,” according to the statement.
However, MOF noted that geopolitical uncertainties in West Asia continue to pose risks to world petroleum price stability.
Meanwhile, the price of subsidised RON95 through Budi95 remains at RM1.99 per liter, with the government bearing a subsidy of RM2.28 per liter, or 53 percent of the unsubsidised price for the period.

According to the MOF, eligible Malaysians can continue to purchase subsidised RON95 and diesel using their MyKad, subject to monthly eligibility limits.

“The Madani Government will continue to take a prudent approach to protect the rakyat from price fluctuations, while ensuring that the country’s fuel supply remains adequate and secure,” the statement added. — Bernama
9eb660ec5ee631f9: GEORGE TOWN, Nov 4 — A one-off payment of RM600 for e-hailing drivers in Penang will be disbursed in 2027, with applications opening in January 2027 through the i-Sejahtera system.
State Infrastructure, Transport and Digital Committee chairman Zairil Khir Johari said the application criteria for the Special E-Hailing Incentive Assistance would be announced next month.
“E-hailing services have become an important component of the urban transport system, supporting first- and last-mile connectivity while providing the public with flexible mobility services.

“In line with the Unity Manifesto that was announced, a payment of RM600 will be disbursed in 2027, with applications to be submitted through the i-Sejahtera system,” he said when winding up the debate on the Supply Bill and the 2027 Development Expenditure Estimates (State Budget 2027) at the State Legislative Assembly sitting today.

Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow, when tabling the 2027 State Budget on Friday (Oct 30), announced that the state government would introduce a one-off Special E-Hailing Incentive Assistance of RM600 for eligible drivers, with an allocation ceiling of RM9 million.

In a separate development, Zairil said the state government had submitted an application to the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) for RM750 million in funding under the Universal Service Provision (USP) Fund to implement the Communication Infrastructure and Digital Connectivity for Penang Smart City initiative.

He said the proposed initiative included the development of about 290 kilometres of fibre-optic network, mainly in Seberang Perai, the expansion of last-mile facilities and communication tower infrastructure and connectivity support for private 5G networks.

He said it would also involve the development of a Network Operations Centre (NOC), artificial intelligence (AI)-based smart asset monitoring and provision of high-speed public WiFi facilities to strengthen the state’s overall digital capabilities.
“As such, the state government hopes that MCMC will give due consideration to and subsequently approve this application for funding to enable the initiative to be implemented in Penang.

2b7435466710e25e: GEORGE TOWN, Nov 4 — Construction of the Mutiara Line Light Rail Transit (LRT) alignment linking Macallum on the island to Penang Sentral in Seberang Perai, including a marine bridge across the Penang Strait, is scheduled to begin in the third quarter of 2027.

13916be253a307f9: BANGKOK, Nov 4 — Five Uighurs detained in Thailand since 2014 are subject to Chinese arrest warrants, the kingdom’s security chief said today, adding that a court would decide if they would be returned to China.
Human rights groups have raised concerns about the men — members of the Muslim minority group who activists say are persecuted in China — after two of them were pardoned by Thailand last month.
They were among more than 300 Uighurs held in Thailand in 2014, most of whom have since left — including a group of around 40 sent last year to China, a move that sparked international outrage.
The five were jailed for trying to escape immigration detention in 2020 and under Thai law have to serve their sentences before deportation.
Two of them were pardoned last month and are in immigration detention awaiting their fate.
“These five have arrest warrants in China and they have no refugee status,” Chaipruak Doungprapat, secretary-general of Thailand’s National Security Council, told reporters today.
He said that if China requests their extradition, Thailand’s foreign ministry would make an assessment and a court would then decide.
“If the court rules that they are guilty, they will be handed over under the extradition treaty,” Chaipruak said.
“If they win, it depends on whether any (other) country is willing to take them.”
Asked today about the fate of the five men, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning did not provide details.

“China and Thailand’s cooperation in combating cross-border criminal activities such as illegal immigration is in line with the two countries’ laws, international law and international practice,” she said.
‘Grave risks’

Thailand is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention, but is bound by the international legal principle of non-refoulement, which bars countries from sending people back to places where their lives or freedom are in danger.
Human Rights Watch warned today that the Uighurs faced “grave risks of torture and other serious abuses” in China, and should be allowed to travel to a safe third country.
Beijing has been accused of detaining more than a million Uighurs and other Muslims since 2017, part of a campaign that the United Nations previously said could constitute crimes against humanity.
China vehemently denies these allegations, saying its policies have boosted economic development and rooted out extremism in the Xinjiang region, where most Uighurs are from.
In letters written by the two pardoned men and shared with AFP by Peace Rights Foundation, which provides them legal representation, they said they do not want to return to China.
“If we go back to China, we and our parents must receive death sentence(s),” one letter says.
“The Uighur people have no human rights and are treated lower than animals.”
It adds: “China is slandering us. We aren’t terrorist(s).”
‘Rather die’
Thailand’s foreign ministry did not immediately reply to emailed questions from AFP.
But a ministry official told a parliament committee on September 16 that both China and a Western country had requested five detained Uighurs be sent to them, according to parliamentary minutes.
Kannavee Suebsang, chairman of Peace Rights Foundation, said defence lawyers have not been given access to the two pardoned men since October 21 when they were moved to immigration custody.
The pair told a Thai human rights commissioner on Wednesday that they want to be resettled in a third country, Kannavee told AFP.
“They refuse to return to China and would rather die first.” — AFP
0e5c092a673c11e0: Attackers tampered with cold-storage settings used by France's civilian blood service after compromising a refrigeration supplier, the organization said.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed the incident on Tuesday, saying its own systems had not been directly targeted. Safeguards prevented any loss of blood products.
The affected equipment stored blood samples and frozen plasma, including plasma intended for transfusion.

"The EFS' monitoring and alarm systems enabled the rapid identification of these anomalies and the implementation of necessary measures to ensure that no blood samples or products were compromised," it said.

"Thus, depending on the circumstances, as soon as the incident occurred, the affected equipment was either brought under control without impacting the products and samples, or neutralized; the products stored in these cold rooms were preventively transferred to other facilities."
The EFS did not name the supplier publicly.
According to reports, attackers changed cold-room temperature settings from -30°C to 110°C. That does not mean the equipment or its contents reached the higher temperature.
The organization added that it notified the country's cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the Ministry of Health.

News about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration devices across Europe emerged on Monday morning after retailers arrived to work, only to find puddles on the floor after cyber criminals activated defrost modes.
Reports of the supermarket attacks describe remotely activated defrost cycles and temperatures as high as 50°C, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food.
The attackers have not been identified. More retailers have reported disruption since the initial disclosures on Monday.

Stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden were the first to report issues, although cases from Estonia, Finland, Germany, Portugal, Romania, and the Netherlands have since been confirmed.

Richard Horne, chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), told BBC Radio 4's Today program on Wednesday that he was aware of "a couple of impacts" in the UK's own food supply chain.

No affected UK businesses have publicly identified themselves, although the British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC that some of its more than 300 members had become "collateral" in the attacks, with two reporting that their fridges had begun defrosting.
The latest wave of cold-store attacks comes a month after the first, which affected French supermarket chains Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others.
Both supermarket waves involved remote interference with refrigeration controls, causing stock losses. Whether the attack affecting EFS used the same access route remains unclear.
Some affected chains identified Danfoss controllers in their systems; others said they did not use the company's equipment.
CERT-FR published an advisory at the time of the attacks urging organizations to remediate vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers.
The attacks in France followed reports of compromises at US military commissaries, which also led to food wastage in August. ®
